def run_n_timesteps(
    time_steps: int,
    reaction: Model,
    transport: cwr.ClearwaterRiverine,
    meteo_params: dict,
    riverine_to_modules: list,
    modules_to_riverine: list,
    modules_to_riverine_matching={},
    concentration_update=None,
    logging=False,
    log_file_name='log',
    logging_interval=5000,
):
    """Function to couple Clearwater Riverine and Modules for n timesteps."""

    # 1. Set up logger
    if logging:
        logger = setup_function_logger(f'{log_file_name}')

    # Loop through all timesteps
    for i in range(1, time_steps):
        if logging:
            if i % logging_interval == 0:
                status = {
                    'timesteps': i,
                    'cwr': transport.mesh.nbytes * 1e-9,
                    'cwm': reaction.dataset.nbytes*1e-9,
                }
                logger.debug(status)

        # 2. Top of timestep: Update transport model
        transport.update(concentration_update)

        # 3. Update state values
        # 3.1 Update using outputs from Clearwater Riverine
        updated_state_values = {}
        for state_variable_name in riverine_to_modules:
            if state_variable_name in modules_to_riverine_matching:
                riverine_key = modules_to_riverine_matching[state_variable_name]
            else:
                riverine_key = state_variable_name
            updated_state_values[state_variable_name] = transport.mesh[riverine_key].isel(
                    time=i,
                    nface=slice(0, transport.mesh.nreal + 1)
            )

        # 3.2 Update meteorological inputs
        for meteo_param in meteo_params.keys():
            updated_state_values[meteo_param] = xr.full_like(
                updated_state_values[riverine_to_modules[0]],
                meteo_params[meteo_param][i]
            )

        # 4. Bottom of timestep: update energy budget (TSM)
        reaction.increment_timestep(updated_state_values)

        # 5. Prepare data for input back into Riverine
        concentration_update = {}
        for variable in modules_to_riverine:
            if variable in modules_to_riverine_matching:
                riverine_key = modules_to_riverine_matching[variable]
            else:
                riverine_key = variable

            reaction.dataset[variable] = reaction.dataset[variable].where(
                ~np.isinf(reaction.dataset[variable]),
                transport.mesh[riverine_key].isel(
                    nface=slice(0, transport.mesh.nreal+1),
                    time=i
                )
            )
            reaction.dataset[variable] = reaction.dataset[variable].fillna(
                transport.mesh[riverine_key].isel(
                    nface=slice(0, transport.mesh.nreal+1),
                    time=i
                )
            )
            concentration_update[riverine_key] = reaction.dataset[variable].isel(seconds=i)

docs.title: ClearWater-Riverine Demo 3 (part 1): Coupling Transport to Water Quality Reactions with ClearWater-Modules¶
docs.text:
Objective: Demonstrate a more complex scenario of coupled transport and reaction models in Sumwere Creek, using the ClearWater-modules to simulate water quality concentrations related to nutrients.

This third notebook builds on the previous two notebooks using ClearWater-riverine provided in demo notebook 1 and 2.

docs.title: Background¶
docs.text: This notebook couples Clearwater-riverine (transport) with Clearwater-modules (reactions) - specifically, the Nutrient Simulation Model I (NSMI). The NSMI is an essential component of ClearWater (Corps Library for Environmental Analysis and Restoration of Watersheds). NSMI plays a crucial role in simulating and predicting water quality constituents concentrations within aquatic ecosystems. The NSMI was designed to conduct an aquatic eutrophication simulation with simplified processes and minimum state variables. The NSMI predicts algae and benthic algae biomass, simple nitrogen and phosphorus cycles, organic carbon, carbonaceous biochemical oxygen demand, dissolved oxygen and pathogen using 16 state variables. These state variables can be selected to be "on" or "off" for custom application of the model.

docs.title: Example Case Study¶
docs.text:
This example shows how to run Clearwater Riverine coupled with Clearwater Modules in a fictional location, "Sumwere Creek" (shown below). The flow field for Sumwere Creek comes from a HEC-RAS 2D model, which has a domain of 2x2 km and a base mesh cell size of 100x100 meters.

The upstream boundary for Sumwere Creek is at the top left of the model domain, flowing into the domain at a constant 3 cms. At the first bend in the creek, there is an additional boundary representing a spring-fed tributary to the creek (1 cms). Further downstream, there is a meander in the stream forming a slow-flowing oxbow lake. There is another boundary flowing into that oxbow lake, representing a powerplant discharge (0.5 cms).

The downstream boundary is a constant stage set at 20.75 meters.

In this example, the focus is on Ammonium (NH4), Nitrate (NO3), Total inorganic phosphorous (TIP), dissolved oxygen (DOX), and Algae [phytoplankton] (Ap) with all other state variables turned off.

All boundary condition concentrations for these five state variables are set to a constant value for the duration of the simulation.

Boundary Condition NH4 (mg/L) NO3 (mg/L) TIP (mg/L) DOX (mg/L) Ap (mg/L) upstream 0.010 0.500 0.050 8.000 10.000 downstream 0.010 0.500 0.050 8.000 10.000 spring-fed 1.800 0.250 0.001 4.000 0.000 powerplant 1.500 1.000 0.060 8.000 200.000

The initial condition concentrations throughout the domain for these state variables are set to the same values as the upstream boundary condition except for Ap within the oxbow lake cells which are set to 200 mg/L.

We simulate this scenario over the course of one full day, using solar radiation data from Arizona in part to compute Ap growth which helps to show off the impacts of NSMI.

At this time, every state variable (including the ones that are turned off) needs to have boundary conditions and initial conditions set for the NSMI model to initialize. The appropriate files, including for state variables switched off, have been added to the simulation directory for this use. It should be noted that place holder values were used for these switched off variables, and the user should modify the values if alternative simulations with these state variables switched on are executed. Since the Clearwater-riverine library was use to initialize the state variables in Clearwater-modules and the code in this notebook intentionally did not pass any information regarding the switched off state variables back to "riverine", the saved results from this model simulaltion will also have results for the turned off state variables, but they are only being advected/diffused and are essentially acting as tracers.

docs.title: ClearWater-Riverine Demo 2: Coupling Transport to Water Quality Reactions with ClearWater-Modules
ClearWater-Riverine Demo 2: Coupling Transport to Water Quality Reactions with ClearWater-Modules¶
docs.text:
Objective: Demonstrate a more complex scenario of coupled transport and reaction models in Sumwere Creek, using the ClearWater-modules to simulate heat exchange with the atmosphere.

This second notebook builds on the introduction to using ClearWater-riverine provided in demo notebook 1.

docs.title: Background¶
docs.text: This notebook couples Clearwater-riverine (transport) with Clearwater-modules (reactions) - specifically, the Temperature Simulation Model (TSM). The Temperature Simulation Module (TSM) is an essential component of ClearWater (Corps Library for Environmental Analysis and Restoration of Watersheds). TSM plays a crucial role in simulating and predicting water temperature within aquatic ecosystems. TSM utilizes a comprehensive energy balance approach to account for various factors contributing to heat inputs and outputs in the water environment. It considers both external forcing functions and heat exchanges occurring at the water surface and the sediment-water interface. The primary contributors to heat exchange at the water surface include shortwave solar radiation, longwave atmospheric radiation, heat conduction from the atmosphere to the water, and direct heat inputs. Conversely, the primary factors that remove heat from the system are longwave radiation emitted by the water, evaporation, and heat conduction from the water to the atmosphere. The core principle behind TSM is the application of the laws of conservation of energy to compute water temperature. This means that the change in heat content of the water is directly related to changes in temperature, which, in turn, are influenced by various heat flux components. The specific heat of water is employed to establish this relationship. Each term of the heat flux equation can be calculated based on the input provided by the user, allowing for flexibility in modeling different environmental conditions

docs.title: Example Case Study¶
docs.text:
This example shows how to run Clearwater Riverine coupled with Clearwater Modules in a fictional location, "Sumwere Creek" (shown below). The flow field for Sumwere Creek comes from a HEC-RAS 2D model, which has a domain of 2x2 km and a base mesh cell size of 100x100 meters.

The upstream boundary for Sumwere Creek is at the top left of the model domain, flowing into the domain at a constant 3 cms. At the first bend in the creek, there is an additional boundary representing a spring-fed tributary to the creek (1 cms). Further downstream, there is a meander in the stream forming a slow-flowing oxbow lake. There is another boundary flowing into that oxbow lake, representing a powerplant discharge (0.5 cms).

The downstream boundary is a constant stage set at 20.75. The upstream inflows have a water temperature of 15 degrees C; the spring-fed creek has constant inflows of 5 C, and the powerplant is steady at 20 C with periodic higher temperature (25 C) discharges in a downstream meander.

We simulate this scenario over the course of two full days, using meteorological parameters from Arizona (extreme temperature swings between night and day) to help show off the impacts of TSM.

In this case, our model timestep dt is equal to 30 seconds. However, by default in Clearwater-Modules, it is 1 day. We will therefore need to define dt:

docs.title: Instantiate Clearwater Modules¶
docs.text:
We instantiate Clearwater Modules with the following:

  • time_steps (required): the number of timesteps to run.
  • initial_state_values (required): our initial conditions of water temperature, cell volumes, and cell surface areas.
  • updateable_static_variables (optional): by default, the meteorological variables are static in TSM. If we want these to update over time, we must provide a list of variables that we want to be updateable as input when instantiating the model.
  • meteo_parameters (optional): intitial meteorological parameters. If not provided, all meteo parameters will fall to default values.
  • temp_parameters (optional): update parameters for the TSM model. If not provided, all temperature parameters will fall to default values.
  • track_dynamic_variables (optional): boolean indicating whether or not the user wants to track all intermediate information used in the calculations. We set this to False to save on memory.
  • use_sed_temp (optional): boolean indicating whether to use the sediment temperature in TSM calculations. We opt to turn this off for simplicity.
  • time_dim (optional): the model timestep

docs.title: Set-Up Coupling Function¶
docs.text:
Now that we have instantiated both our Clearwater-Riverine and Clearwater-Modules models, we can couple them. We will do so using the run_n_timesteps function, which runs n number of timesteps, with the following process:

  1. Optionally sets up a logger.
  2. Top of the timestep: Increment the transport model (Riverine). After the first timestep, information from Clearwater-Modules will be passed back into Clearwater-Riverine.
  3. Create inputs for Clearwater Modules with outputs from Clearwater Riverine and meteorological data
  4. Bottom of the tiemestep: Increment the reaction model (Modules).
  5. Create inputs for Clearwater Riverine with outputs from Clearwater Modules.

The inputs for the function are as follows:

  • time_steps: The number of timesteps to run.
  • reaction: The Clearwater-Modules model (instantiated above)
  • transport: The Clearwater-Riverine model (instantiated above)
  • meteo_params: Meteorological inputs (defined above)
  • riverine_to_modules: A list of inputs to modules for the specified model
  • modules_to_riverine: A list of inputs from riverine back to modules.
  • modules_to_riverine_matching: A dictionary mapping the names of clearwater modules variable names (keys) to clearwater riverine module names (values). Only needed where the values are different.
  • concentration_update: this will be None on the first timestep; it will get updated by Clearwater Modules.
  • logging: Boolean to log (True) or not (False). False by default.
  • log_file_name: Name of log file. log by default.
  • logging_interval: Number of timesteps that should pass between logs. Selecting a small number will slow down the model.

docs.title: Run the Coupling Function¶
docs.text:
Earlier in the notebook, we set up most of what we need to couple the models. However, we still need to define a few key inputs that help pass information back and forth between Clearwater Riverine with the following input parameters:

  • riverine_to_modules: We are passing water temperature, surface area, and volume from Riverine to Modules.
  • modules_to_riverine: We are passing water temperature from Modules back to Riverine.
  • modules_to_riverine_matching: Water temperature and surface area are named differently in the two models. We'll need to use this dictionary to show that link.

ClearWater-Riverine Demo 1: Getting Started with Conservative Transport¶
docs.text:
Objective: Demonstrate how to use the ClearWater-riverine library to simulate 2D conservative transport (advection and mixing) on Sumwere Creek.

A second demo notebook couples ClearWater-riverine to ClearWater-modules to simulate water quality reaction processes, such as heat balance for water temperature modeling.

docs.title: Background¶
docs.text: ClearWater-Riverine is a two-dimensional (2D) water quality model for complex river systems and floodplains. It is developed by the Environmental Laboratory, U.S Army Engineer Research and Development Center (ERDC). The intent of this model is to simulate the transport (advection and mixing) of heat and water quality constituents in riverine systems by integrating it with ERDC's ClearWater (Corps Library for Environmental Analysis and Restoration of Watersheds) modules.

docs.text: Carefully follow our Installation Instructions.

docs.text:
This example shows how to run Clearwater Riverine in a fictional location, "Sumwere Creek" (shown below). The flow field for Sumwere Creek comes from a HEC-RAS 2D model, which has a domain of 2x2 kilometers and a base mesh of 100x100 meters

The upstream boundary for Sumwere Creek is at the top left of the model domain, flowing into the domain at a constant 3 cms. At the first bend in the creek, there is an additional boundary representing a spring-fed tributary to the creek (1 cms). Further downstream, there is a meander in the stream forming a slow-flowing oxbow lake. There is another boundary flowing into that oxbow lake, representing a powerplant discharge (0.5 cms).

The downstream boundary is a constant stage set at 20.75 m. The upstream inflows have a water temperature of 15 degrees C; the spring-fed creek has constant inflows of 5 C, and the powerplant is steady at 20 C with periodic higher temperature (25 C) discharges in a downstream meander.

There are two ways to instantiate a Clearwater Riverine model. Here, we will set it up using the following inputs:

  • flow_field_file_path: input the path to the model flow field
  • constituent_dict: a dictionary defining all constituents, as well as filepaths for their initial and boundary conditions

docs.title: Writing/using a simple Model sub-class example¶
docs.text:
In this example we will be writing a base.Model sub-class that calculates the annual carbon sequestration in a forest for a given year timestep.

Note: Do not take the calculation too literally! I got it off ChatGPT in order to find a good, simple example for the code.

docs.title: Next, use the register_variable decorator to add a few variables¶
docs.text:
To do this, make a sub-class of base.Variable but with the decorator pointed at the model(s) you want to add the variables too. Note that the models argument of the decorator must be either a single sub-class of base.Model, or a list of them.

Next, just write instances of the new base.Variable sub-class. Each variable's use attribute must be set to static, dynamic, and state. Read below about what this means / how you should split up your variables.

Note that anything that needs to be calculated or input into a model should be encapsulated by a variable!

docs.title: Add our static variables¶
docs.text:
Working Definition: Static variables are any variables that will not change across the course of a simulation, regardless of how many time-steps are run.

Note that one can update static variables if they really want to by re-initializing the model class and providing new static variable inputs.

Here we will use the following static variables:

  1. Net Primary Productivity (NPP): The average annual NPP of the forest ecosystem (g/m²/year).
  2. Carbon Content: The fraction of NPP that is composed of carbon (usually around 50%, but it can vary).

docs.title: Add our dynamic variables¶
docs.text:
Working Definition: Dynamic variables are any intermediate variable calculation that don't need to be passed to the next timestep. All dynamic variables need to be associated with a function via the optional Variable.process attribute. This "process" function is used to calculate them. Importantly, the arguments of said function should match the variable names that will be passed in!

In this simple example we will have only one dynamic variable:

  1. Annual carbon sequestration (delta_C_annual):

    delta_C_annual = npp * carbon_content * forest_area

docs.title: Add our state variable¶
docs.text:
Working Definition: A state variable is the main input/output to each timestep. Notably, it can be updated between timesteps to allow interaction with other models. Our model needs to be initialized with state variable values, and no matter what settings are used in initialization, the state variable is stored in our main dataset (keep reading to see this).

Our state variable is the total carbon stock of the forest, which is updated each year:

  1. Total carbon stock (C_total):

    C_total = C_total + delta_C_annual

State variables also require a process function.

docs.title: Now let's instantiate our new model¶
docs.text: To instantiate a model we need to pass in a dictionary with our initial state variable values, any non-default changes to our static variables, and any other optional config settings.

docs.title: All instantiated models have static, dynamic, and state variable properties¶
One can access their "computation order" which is calculated using a "dependency tree" approach in sorter.py¶
Running a timestep¶
docs.text: All timesteps can be run independently. Optionally, one can update the state values with a float or a xarray.DataArray.

docs.title: Running a loop of timesteps¶
docs.text:
Here we run 100 years of our model with the following hypothetical:

  • For the first 50 years deforestation reduces forest area incrementally.
  • 50 years in, a program begins that ends deforestation, and the forest grows back incrementally.

This demonstrates how we can update state variables to interact with other models!

docs.text: Now that we understand how the code architecture works, we can explore a real example.

docs.text: Initial state variable values are always required. To see the names/info of a model's state variables, we can use Model.get_state_variables().

Ohio River Model¶
docs.text:
This notebook showcases the Clearwater Riverine water quality model, which uses hydrodynamic outputs from HEC-RAS 2D in order to perform advection-diffusion water quality calculations. This model is in the clearwater_riverine package (in development).

Environmental Fluid Dynamics Code (EFDC) is a surface water modeling system developed by the EPA that can simulate water quality constituent transport in rivers, stratified estuaries, lakes, and coastal seas. Since EFDC is a widely used and trusted water quality model, we can compare results from an EFDC model to results from a comparable system in a Clearwater Riverine model to demonstrate this new model's efficacy. This demonstration leverages a RAS model of the Ohio River that was created based on an EFDC model of the Ohio River that modeled E. coli transport through the system as a conservative dye. The RAS model was created to mirror the EFDC model, including the 2D model mesh, the initial conditions, and the boundary conditions. However, there are some key differences between the two models (e.g., the cells aren't perfectly aligned, the modeling timestep is different, and the spatial extent is different). It is then fed into the Clearwater Riverine water quality model, which simulates advection and diffusion of E. coli through the model domain.

This notebook follows the following structure:

  1. Run the Clearwater Riverine water quality model using the Ohio River RAS model output.
  2. Load EFDC water quality results.
  3. Compare Clearwater Riverine water quality results to EFDC water quality results to demonstrate that the Clearwater Riverine model produces similar results.

docs.title: Package Imports¶
docs.text: Be sure to install the clearwater_riverine environment from the environment.yml - instructions are provided on the ReadMe of the Clearwater-riverine repo.

docs.title: RAS File Paths¶
docs.text: Define the file path to the RAS2D HDF output file of interest. In this example, the HEC-RAS model output for the Ohio River is saved to the following path:

docs.title: Set-Up Model Mesh¶
docs.text:
The code below creates a ClearwaterRiverine model. Initializing this model requires two arguments:

  • fpath: the filepath to the RAS2D HDF output (defined in the code block above).
  • diffusion_coefficient: assumed diffusion coefficient for the entire model domain (arbitrarily set to 0.1 here)

docs.title: Define Initial Conditions¶
docs.text:
Initial conditions for the Clear Water model simulation of the Ohio River were developed as follows: A 5 ft raster was made from the EFDC shape file with the E. coli initial conditions and then a zonal statistic average was calculated for the HEC-RAS cells, creating the timeseries imported here.

To set up the initial conditions in a Clearwater Riverine model, use the intitial_condtions method, which accepts a CSV file with Cell_Index and Concentration as the column headers.

docs.title: Define Boundary Conditions¶
docs.text:
Use the boundary_conditions method to pass a CSV containing boundary condition information, with should have the following columns:

  • RAS2D_TS_Name: name of boundary condition in the HEC-RAS model
  • Datetime: date and time of boundary condition
  • Concentration: concentration (mass per volume)

The current set-up assumes that each timestep in the RAS model will have a concentration in this CSV file and no further interpolation/data cleaning is required. We will likely want to build out this functionality to accept any datetimes and properly interpolate the data to fit the RAS model, rather than requiring users to do all clean-up and interpolation on their own.

The boundary conditions were developed based on data in the EFDC model so that we can directly compare model output.

docs.title: Run Model¶
docs.text:
Run the RAS2D water quality model using simulate_wq, which accepts the following (optional) parameters:

  • input_mass_units: User-defined mass units for concentration timeseries based on initial / boundary conditions. Assumes mg if no value is specified.
  • input_volume_units: User-defined volume units for concentration timeseries based on initial / boundary conditions. Assumes L if no value is specified.
  • input_liter_conversion: If concentration inputs (initial / boundary conditions) are not in mass/L, supply the conversion factor to convert the volume unit to liters.
  • save: Boolean indicating whether the file should be saved. Default is to not save the output.
  • fpath_out: Filepath where the output file should be stored. Default to save in current directory.
  • fname_out: Filename of saved output.

The unit info should probably be moved to the boundary condition / initial condition setup and also potentially needs to be re-thought out.

In this example, the input mass units are cfu (colony forming unit) since we are modelling E. coli, and the input volume units are 100 mL. We therefore have to provide the input_liter_conversion parameter to correctly convert our input units to liters, which is the assumed unit in all calculations.

docs.title: Quick Plot¶
docs.text: If you want to quickly plot the model results, the quick_plot method takes the cell centroids and plots them in a scatter plot.

docs.title: Detailed Polygon Plot¶
docs.text: We can use the plot() method to plot a more detailed mesh. For this plotting function, you must specifiy the projection of the HEC-RAS model.

docs.title: Example Save to HTML¶
docs.text: The code below shows how to save the plot as an interactive HTML file. These cells will be saved as raw cells because saving the html takes a long time. However, useres can convert these raw cells to code blocks if they would like to choose to save the file to HTML.

docs.title: Example Save to Gif¶
docs.text: Limit the timeframe so that it can be converted from a HoloMap from a DynamicMap and then exported to a gif. These cells will be saved as raw cells because saving a gif takes a long time, but users can convert the raw cells to code blocks if they would like to choose to save a gif.

docs.title: Load EFDC Model¶
docs.text: Now we need to load the EFDC model results of the Ohio River so that we have a point of comparison for the Clearwater Riverine water quality output.

docs.title: Process EFDC Data¶
docs.text: Now we must align the date range of EFDC to match with HEC-RAS, since the models were run over different time extents. Furthermore, the model domain and the model results (concentrations and timesteps) are currently in separate files. In this section we also combine the output data with the EFDC model mesh into a single geopandas dataframe.

docs.title: Make Domains Comparable¶
docs.text:
You can see from the plots above that the model domains are not aligned; the HEC-RAS model and corresponding Clearwater Riverine model have a much more limited spatial extent. The following code is used to limit the EFDC spatial domain to align with the Clearwater Riverine spatial domain.

We start by dissolving the Clearwater Riverine boundary into a single polygon so that we can identify all EFDC polygons that fall within the Clearwater Riverine domain:

docs.title: Side By Side Comparison Plots¶
docs.text: Create side by side comparison plots.

docs.title: Compare Locations¶
docs.text:
When we look at the side by side maps above, the model results from EFDC and Clearwater Riverine look similar! However, now we want to create timeseries plots for each cell that will provide a quantitative comparison of results.

First, we must link EFDC cells to Clearwater Riverine cells to provide approximate cell to cell / location to location comparisons. We do this by finding the centroid of each Clearwater Riverine cell and then find the closest EFDC cell using a spatial join.

docs.title: Difference Plot¶
docs.text: Plot the difference in concentration for each cell.

docs.title: ClearWater-Riverine Demo 3 (part 2): Coupling Transport to Water Quality Reactions with ClearWater-Modules¶
docs.text: This notebook can load the saved model results form the part one notebook or load previously saved model results that were downloaded from Google Drive.

docs.title: Import Model Results¶
docs.text: The files downloaded from Google Drive in the part one notebook of this example has a previous set of riverine/NSMI model results that were included just in case you were not able to get the model to run or if you are not willing to wait until your simulation is complete and you are eager to see some plots of the results.

docs.title: Plot Model Results¶
docs.text:
Clearwater Riverine has developed some convenience functions for plotting outputs that leverage the HoloViz suite of dynamic visualization libraries.

  • ClearwaterRiverine.plot() is a custom function for mapping outputs over the RAS-2D model grid.

In addition, each ClearwaterRiverine model instance includes model data in native xarray and pandas formats, for plotting directly:

  • ClearwaterRiverine.mesh (xr.Dataset): Unstructured model mesh containing relevant HEC-RAS outputs, calculated parameters required for advection-diffusion calculations, and water quality ouptuts (e.g., concentration). The unstructured mesh follows UGRID CF Conventions.
  • ClearwaterRiverine.boundary_data (pd.DataFrame): Information on RAS model boundaries, extracted directly from HEC-RAS 2D output. We can therefore plot data directly from these underlying data structures.

docs.title: Create Line Plot Function¶
docs.text: By creating Holoviews Curve plots for a specified list of cells and combining into an HoloViews Overlay.

docs.title: Save a Dynamic Map Plot as an *.html File¶
Standalone TSM
docs.text:
This step will load in the entire clearwater modules library, which has all the source code necessary to run the modules, including the various python dependencies used to make the calculations, such as numpy and xarray.

In [17]: Copied!

import clearwater_modules.sorter as sorter
import random
import warnings
import xarray as xr
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
import clearwater_modules as cwm import clearwater_modules.sorter as sorter import random import warnings import xarray as xr warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

Importing the clearwater_modules repository will automatically run the base.py file that defines the Model class. It will also define a child of that class called the EnergyBudget class, which is defined in the model.py file. This class has the same functionality of the general Model class, but has attributes and methods for the expected inputs for TSM. The TSM inputs are broken down into two dictionaries, which are titled Meteorological and Temperature. The EnergyBudget class intitializes the TSM inputs with default values and sets them as class attributes for instances of the EnergyBudget class.

The default TSM values are defined in the TSM constants.py file, which is imported with cwm. Run the following cell to make sure that the TSM subfolder from the clearwater_modules repository successfully imports.

Similar to the module-engine, the input variables are defined as class instances. These instances are defined in the static_variables.py file. Whereas the Temperature and Meteorological dictionaries set the actual values for the TSM inputs, the static variable class instances define how these values will be passed around in the model. As suggested by the word static, once set by the dictionaries, the values do not change throughout the model run. Run the code below to view the static variables used in the TSM module. You will notice that static_variables.py has definitions for all the variables assigned values by the Temperature and Meteorological dictionaries. You will also see at the top of the file a decorator above the class definition that calls a function called register_variable. This function links these variables to the EnergyBudget model.

The state_variables.py file instatiates the variable for water temperature (TwaterC), surface area, and volume. The state variables are treated differently because their values will be updated at every computational timestep. These variables are designed to be passed back and forth between the TSM module and a hydrodynamic model, and their values will change at every timestep based on the transport taking place in the linked hydrodynamic model. For TwaterC, the value will also change based on computations made in clearwater_modules. As stated previously, this example notebook will provide inputs for these variables in a dictionary in order to run the model. However, the dictionary inputs are a simplification of linking to external models. Run the code below to view the state variable file. Notice that the state variables are linked to the EnergyBudget model using the decorator function. Also notice that the state variable instances have a property called process. This property allows the value of the variable instance to be updated using a function that shares the name of what is set equal to the process property.

The processes.py file contains all of the functions required to compute the heat flux of a single cell. This is where the process functions that update the state variables are defined. However, there are many intermediate process functions that must be computed before calculating the water temperature change. These intermediate functions calculate dynamic_variables, which are used to calculate components of heat flux, which are ultimately added together to compute a total net heat flux. import warnings
import numba
import numpy as np
import xarray as xr
from clearwater_modules.shared.processes import (
    celsius_to_kelvin,
)


def air_temp_k(
    air_temp_c: xr.DataArray,
) -> xr.DataArray:
    """Calculate air temperature (K).

    Args:
        air_temp_c: Air temperature (C)
    """
    return celsius_to_kelvin(air_temp_c)


def water_temp_k(
    water_temp_c: xr.DataArray,
) -> xr.DataArray:
    """Calculate water temperature (K).

    Args:
        water_temp_c: Water temperature (C)
    """
    return celsius_to_kelvin(water_temp_c)


def mixing_ratio_air(
    eair_mb: xr.DataArray,
    pressure_mb: xr.DataArray,
) -> xr.DataArray:
    """Calculate air mixing ratio (unitless).

    Args:
        eair_mb: Vapour pressure of air (mb)
        pressure_mb: Atmospheric pressure (mb)
    
    References: 
    
    """
    return 0.622 * eair_mb / (pressure_mb - eair_mb)


def density_air(
    pressure_mb: xr.DataArray,
    air_temp_k: xr.DataArray,
    mixing_ratio_air: xr.DataArray,
) -> xr.DataArray:
    """Calculate air density (kg/m^3).

    Args:
        pressure_mb: Atmospheric pressure (mb)
        air_temp_k: Air temperature (K)
        mixing_ratio_air: Air mixing ratio (unitless)
    """
    return (
        0.348 *
        (pressure_mb / air_temp_k) *
        (1.0 + mixing_ratio_air) / (1.0 + 1.61 * mixing_ratio_air)

    )

def mf_density_water(
    water_temp_c: xr.DataArray
) -> xr.DataArray:
    """
    Compute density of water (kg/m3) as a function of water temperature (Celsius)
    """

    # logger.debug(f'mf_density_water({water_temp_c:.2f})')

    return (
        999.973 *
        (1.0 - (
            (
                (water_temp_c - 3.9863) *
                (water_temp_c - 3.9863) *
                (water_temp_c + 288.9414)
            ) /
            (
                508929.2 *
                (water_temp_c + 68.12963)
            )
        ))
    )


def mf_esat_mb(
    water_temp_k: xr.DataArray,
    a0: xr.DataArray,
    a1: xr.DataArray,
    a2: xr.DataArray,
    a3: xr.DataArray,
    a4: xr.DataArray,
    a5: xr.DataArray,
    a6: xr.DataArray,
) -> xr.DataArray:
    """
    Compute the saturation vapor pressure as a function of water temperature (Kelvin)

    Fitting parameters for vapor pressure are defined in:
    Brutsaert (1982) Evaporation into the Atmosphere, p42.
    """

    return (
        a0 +
        water_temp_k *
        (
            a1 +
            water_temp_k *
            (
                a2 +
                water_temp_k * (
                    a3 +
                    water_temp_k *
                    (a4 + water_temp_k * (a5 + water_temp_k * a6))
                )
            )
        )
    )


def mf_density_air_sat(
    water_temp_k: xr.DataArray, 
    esat_mb: float, 
    pressure_mb: float
) -> xr.DataArray:
    """
    Compute the density of saturated air at water surface temperature.

    Parameters:
        water_temp_k (float):        Water temperature (Kelvin)
        esat_mb (float):        Saturation vapor pressure in millibars
        pressure_mb (float):    Air pressure in millibars

    Returns:
        Density of saturated air at water surface temperature (kg/m3, float)
    """

    # logger.debug(f'mf_density_air_sat({water_temp_k:.2f}, {esat_mb:.2f}, {pressure_mb:.2f})')

    mixing_ratio_sat = 0.622 * esat_mb / (pressure_mb - esat_mb)
    return 0.348 * (pressure_mb / water_temp_k) * (1.0 + mixing_ratio_sat) / (1.0 + 1.61 * mixing_ratio_sat)


def ri_number(
    gravity: xr.DataArray,
    density_air: xr.DataArray,
    density_air_sat: xr.DataArray,
    wind_speed: xr.DataArray,
) -> xr.DataArray:
    """Calculates the Richardson Number.

    Args:
        gravity: Gravity (m/s2)
        density_air: Density of air (kg/m3)
        density_air_sat: Saturation density of air (kg/m3)
        wind_speed: Wind speed (m/s)
    """
    return (
        gravity *
        (density_air - density_air_sat) *
        2.0 / (density_air * (wind_speed**2.0))
    )


def ri_function(
    ri_number: xr.DataArray
) -> np.ndarray:
    """Calculates the Richardson Function from the Richardson Number.
    Richardson Number:
        Unstable: 0.01 >= ri_function
        Stable: 0.01 <= ri_function < 2
        Neutral: -0.01 <  ri_function < 0.01
    """
    warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=RuntimeWarning)

    # NOTE: conditions are evaluated in the order of the original code
    # TODO: refactor into a single set of conditions, once testing is in place
    ri_number_bounded: np.ndarray = np.select(
        condlist=[
            ri_number > 2.0,
            ri_number < -1.0,
        ],
        choicelist=[
            2.0,
            -1.0,
        ],
        default=ri_number,
    )
    out: np.ndarray = np.select(
        condlist=[
            (ri_number_bounded < 0.0) & (ri_number_bounded >= -0.01),  # neutral
            (ri_number_bounded < 0.0) & (ri_number_bounded < -0.01),  # unstable
            (ri_number_bounded >= 0.0) & (ri_number_bounded <= 0.01),  # neutral
            (ri_number_bounded >= 0.0) & (ri_number_bounded > 0.01),  # stable
        ],
        choicelist=[
            1.0,                                         # neutral
            (1.0 - 22.0 * ri_number_bounded) ** 0.80,    # unstable
            1.0,                                         # neutral
            (1.0 + 34.0 * ri_number_bounded) ** (-0.80),  # stable
        ],
    )
    warnings.filterwarnings("default", category=RuntimeWarning)
    return out


def mf_latent_heat_vaporization(
    water_temp_k: xr.DataArray
) -> xr.DataArray:
    """
    Compute the latent heat of vaporization (J/kg) as a function of water temperature (Kelvin)
    """

    return 2499999 - 2385.74 * water_temp_k


def mf_cp_water(
    water_temp_c: xr.DataArray
) -> xr.DataArray:
    """
    Compute the specific heat of water (J/kg/K) as a function of water temperature (Celsius).
    This is used in computing the source/sink term.
    """
    # polynomial logic, this produced nearly identical outputs for the range of temperatures tested
    # See discussion about the two methods: https://github.com/EcohydrologyTeam/ClearWater-modules/pull/44
    # return (
    #    (4.65e-6 * water_temp_c - 0.001) *
    #    (water_temp_c + 0.085858) *
    #    (water_temp_c - 3.1331) *
    #    water_temp_c +
    #    4219.793
    # )
    return np.select(
        condlist=[
            water_temp_c <= 0.0,
            water_temp_c <= 5.0,
            water_temp_c <= 10.0,
            water_temp_c <= 15.0,
            water_temp_c <= 20.0,
            water_temp_c <= 25.0,
        ],
        choicelist=[
            4218.0,
            4202.0,
            4192.0,
            4186.0,
            4182.0,
            4180.0,
        ],
        default=4178.0,
    )


def emissivity_air(
    air_temp_k: xr.DataArray,
) -> xr.DataArray:
    """Calculate air emissivity (unitless).

    Args:
        air_temp_k: Air temperature (K)
    """
    return 0.00000937 * air_temp_k**2.0


def wind_function(
    ri_function: xr.DataArray,
    wind_a: xr.DataArray,
    wind_b: xr.DataArray,
    wind_c: xr.DataArray,
    wind_speed: xr.DataArray,
) -> xr.DataArray:
    """Calculate wind function (unitless) for latent and sensible heat.

    Args:
        ri_function: Richardson function (unitless)
        wind_a: Wind function coefficient (unitless)
        wind_b: Wind function coefficient (unitless)
        wind_c: Wind function coefficient (unitless)
        wind_speed: Wind speed (m/s)
    """
    return (
        ri_function * (
            (wind_a / 1000000.0) +
            (wind_b / 1000000.0) *
            (wind_speed**wind_c)
        )
    )


def mf_q_longwave_down(
    air_temp_k: xr.DataArray,
    emissivity_air: xr.DataArray,
    cloudiness: xr.DataArray,
    stefan_boltzmann: xr.DataArray,
) -> xr.DataArray:
    """
    Compute downwelling longwave radiation (W/m2)

    Parameters:
        air_temp_k (float):              Air temperature (Kelvin)
        emissivity_air (float):     Emissivity of air (unitless)
        cloudiness (float):         Cloudiness (fraction)

    Returns:
        Downwelling longwave radiation (W/m2, float)
    """

    return (1.0 + 0.17 * cloudiness**2) * emissivity_air * stefan_boltzmann * air_temp_k**4.0


def mf_q_longwave_up(
    water_temp_k: xr.DataArray,
    emissivity_water: xr.DataArray,
    stefan_boltzmann: xr.DataArray,
) -> xr.DataArray:
    """
    Compute upwelling longwave radiation (W/m2) as a function of water temperature (Kelvin)
    """

    # logger.debug(f'mf_q_longwave_up({water_temp_k:.2f})')

    return emissivity_water * stefan_boltzmann * water_temp_k**4.0


def q_latent(
    pressure_mb: xr.DataArray,
    density_water: xr.DataArray,
    lv: xr.DataArray,
    wind_function: xr.DataArray,
    esat_mb: xr.DataArray,
    eair_mb: xr.DataArray,
) -> xr.DataArray:
    """Latent heat flux (W/m^2).

    Args:
        pressure_mb: Atmospheric pressure (mb)
        density_water: Water density (kg/m^3)
        lv: Latent heat of vaporization (J/kg)
        wind_function: Wind function (unitless)
        esat_mb: Saturation vapour pressure (mb)
        eair_mb: Vapour pressure of air (mb)
    """
    return (
        (0.622 / pressure_mb) *
        lv *
        density_water *
        wind_function *
        (esat_mb - eair_mb)
    )


def q_sensible(
    wind_kh_kw: xr.DataArray,
    cp_air: xr.DataArray,
    density_water: xr.DataArray,
    wind_function: xr.DataArray,
    air_temp_k: xr.DataArray,
    water_temp_k: xr.DataArray,
) -> xr.DataArray:
    # TODO: check if the return units are correct
    """Sensible heat flux (W/m2).

    Args:
        wind_kh_kw: Diffusivity ratio (unitless)
        ri_function: Richardson number (unitless)
        cp_air: Specific heat of air (J/kg/K)
        density_water: Water density (kg/m^3)
        wind_function: Wind function (unitless)
        air_temp_k: Air temperature (K)
        water_temp_k: Water temperature (K)
    """
    return (
        wind_kh_kw *
        cp_air *
        density_water *
        wind_function *
        (air_temp_k - water_temp_k)
    )


def q_sediment(
    use_sed_temp: xr.DataArray,
    pb: xr.DataArray,
    cps: xr.DataArray,
    alphas: xr.DataArray,
    h2: xr.DataArray,
    sed_temp_c: xr.DataArray,
    water_temp_c: xr.DataArray,
) -> xr.DataArray:
    """Sediment heat flux (W/m^2).

    Args:
        use_sed_temp: Whether to calculate sed temp or not (boolean)
        pb: Sediment bulk density (kg/m^3)
        cps: Sediment specific heat (J/kg/K)
        alphas: Sediment thermal diffusivity (m^2/s)
        h2: Sediment active layer thickness (m)
        sed_temp_c: Sediment temperature (C)
        water_temp_c: Water temperature (C)
    """
    # 86400 converts the sediment thermal diffusivity from units of m^2/d to m^2/s
    return np.where(
        use_sed_temp,
        (
            pb * cps * alphas / 0.5 / h2 *
            (sed_temp_c - water_temp_c) / 86400.0
        ),
        0.0,
    )


def q_net(
    q_sensible: xr.DataArray,
    q_latent: xr.DataArray,
    q_longwave_up: xr.DataArray,
    q_longwave_down: xr.DataArray,
    q_solar: xr.DataArray,
    q_sediment: xr.DataArray,
    dt: xr.DataArray,
) -> xr.DataArray:
    """Net heat flux (W/m^2).

    Args:
        q_sensible: Sensible heat flux (W/m^2)
        q_latent: Latent heat flux (W/m^2)
        q_longwave_up: Upward longwave radiation (W/m^2)
        q_longwave_down: Downward longwave radiation (W/m^2)
        q_solar: Solar radiation (W/m^2)
        q_sediment: Sediment heat flux (W/m^2)
        dt: Change in time (days)
    """
    return (
        q_sensible +
        q_solar +
        q_sediment +
        q_longwave_down -
        q_longwave_up -
        q_latent
    ) * 86400 * dt


def dTdt_water_c(
    q_net: xr.DataArray,
    surface_area: xr.DataArray,
    volume: xr.DataArray,
    density_water: xr.DataArray,
    cp_water: xr.DataArray,
) -> xr.DataArray:
    """Water temperature change (C).

    Args:
        q_net: Net heat flux (W/m^2)
        surface_area: Surface area (m^2)
        volume: Volume (m^3)
        density_water: Water density (kg/m^3)
        cp_water: Water specific heat (J/kg/K)
    """
    return (
        q_net *
        surface_area /
        (volume * density_water * cp_water)
    )


def t_water_c(
    water_temp_c: xr.DataArray,
    dTdt_water_c: xr.DataArray,
) -> xr.DataArray:
    """Water temperature (C).

    Args:
        t_water_c: Water temperature (C)
        dt_water_c: Water temperature change (C)
    """
    return water_temp_c + dTdt_water_c

Dynamic variables are computed by the process functions and then used as inputs to subsequent processes until the new TwaterC has been calculated. These variables are defined similarly to state variables. They are instances of a class Variable that gets registered to the EnergyBudget model, and have a process property that links them to a function which defines their value. Unlike static and state variables, dynamic variables do not need initial values, and are not designed to get passed outside of a module computation step. In the model implementation, there is an option to track or not track dynamic variables in memory. The default is to track dynamic variable values, which can be useful for seeing which components have the strongest influence on the overall temperature flux. The order in which dynamic variables must be calculated is determined by the sorter.py file defined in the main folder of the clearwater_modules repository. This file inspects the arguments for each process function, and checks if these arguments are available in the list of module inputs (static variables with default values, or state variables) or if the arguments are computed during the module run (dynamic variables). The sorter will then put the processes in order to ensure that each process will have all its input arguments defined prior to being called. The sorter.py file is called when the module is run.

Now that the different types of module variables and processes have been defined, we can set up an example module, and run one timestep. To do so, we must create an instance of the EnergyBudget model-class that has our desired model inputs. There are a few other options that we set when instatiating the model-class. First, we must determine the number of timesteps we plan to run, by defining the time_steps attribute. This is done to improve module computation performance. The size of each timestep is not explicitly defined, and assumed to equal 1 second, but is another variable that should be pulled from the linked hydrodynamic model. Second, we define the initial values for the state variables and static variables (meteorologic and temperature) using dictionaries. The state variables must have initial values provided upon instantiation of the EnergyBudget model. Static variables have default values that will be used if no dictionary is provided upon instantiation. Finally, a few computation options need to be defined. These are track_dynamic_variables, a boolean attribute which controls whether or not we want to save the value of dynamic variables for each timestep, hotstart_dataset, which is another way to initialize EnergyBudget using precomputed variables NOT CLEAR IF FUNCTIONING**, and an attribute called time_dim, which is the name of the time dimension. Run the codeblock below to instantiate an EnergyBudget model.

The tsm_model instance that we define above has all the information we need to compute the change in water temperature given the conditions we have defined. Run the code below to view the x-array data structure that holds all of this information. The x-array structure displays the dimensions of data that we are tracking. Since there is only one computation cell, we only see one entry for the x and y dimension respectively. We set our time_steps = 1, which is reflected by the two entries in the Seconds dimension: the values for the initial conditions, and the values of the tracked variables after that 1 timestep is run. Expand Data variables to view the state, static, and dynamic variables. Since this dataset reflects initial conditions before a timestep has been run, you will see nan values entered as placeholders for the dynamic variables and for the second column of state variables. There is only one column of data for static variables, as these to do not change over the timesteps.

docs.title: This notebook will introduce users to the Temperature Simulation Module TSM and familiarize them with the module architecture, inputs, and outputs. It will demonstrate how different types of variables are defined and then connected to the module's computational engine. TSM is built in an object-oriented framework. The module engine, which calculates the temperature change for a given timestep, is based on a parent-class titled Model. Module inputs are class attributes, and functions that update the input values are class methods.¶

These modules are designed to compute fluxes for a single computation cell, which is assumed to be completely homogeneous. The dimensions of the cell, such as depth, volume, and surface area, are defined in this example as inputs for the modules. When implemented with a hydrodynamic model, cell dimensions will be pulled from the hydrodynamic model.¶
If you get ModuleNotFoundError:¶

ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'clearwater_modules'

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
This section introduces the ClearWater framework and walks new users from installation through a first coupled simulation. The Getting Started pages assume a working knowledge of Python and scientific computing with numpy and xarray, but they do not assume prior experience with HEC-RAS or water quality modeling.

Start with the Overview to understand how the three ClearWater packages fit together, then follow the Installation guide to set up a working environment. The Quickstart tutorial walks through a minimal end-to-end simulation that couples ClearWater-Riverine with the Temperature Simulation Module (TSM).

docs.title: Contents
docs.text:
• Overview -- Architecture of the ClearWater framework, the three-package design, and the Process-based execution model.
  • Installation -- Prerequisites, environment setup, and installation from source for each of the three ClearWater packages.
  • Quickstart -- A minimal tutorial that configures, runs, and inspects the results of a coupled Riverine plus TSM simulation.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
This page describes how to install the three ClearWater packages for development and use. ClearWater is pre-release software under active development at ERDC, so the recommended installation method is from source against the latest main or feature branch of each repository.

Pre-release software

ClearWater is under active development. APIs may change between commits, and the packages are not yet published to PyPI or conda-forge. Installation is from source only.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
ClearWater requires the following:

  • Python 3.11 or later for ClearWater-Modules.
  • Python 3.10 or later for ClearWater-Riverine.
  • conda (via Miniconda or Anaconda) or an equivalent environment manager such as mamba or pixi.
  • Git for cloning the source repositories.
  • A working installation of HEC-RAS 2D (Windows) or a pre-computed HEC-RAS plan HDF file, if you plan to use ClearWater-Riverine.

conda installation location

Install Miniconda or Anaconda in your local user directory. Do not install for all users; system-wide installs create persistent permission problems when creating environments.

docs.title: Installation Steps
docs.text: The recommended workflow is to clone all three repositories into a common parent directory, create a single conda environment from ClearWater-modules/environment.yml, and install each package in editable mode with pip.

docs.title: 1. Clone the Source Repositories
docs.text:
Clone the three repositories from the EcohydrologyTeam GitHub organization:

git clone https://github.com/EcohydrologyTeam/ClearWater-modules.git
git clone https://github.com/EcohydrologyTeam/ClearWater-riverine.git
git clone https://github.com/EcohydrologyTeam/ClearWater-data.git

Development branches

The unified Process ABC architecture and the clearwater_modules_v2 package live on feature branches rather than main. Check the ClearWater-modules repository for the current active development branch before installing if you intend to use the v2 API.

docs.title: 2. Create a Conda Environment
docs.text:
Create a conda environment from the environment.yml file in the ClearWater-modules repository. This environment contains xarray, zarr, numpy, numba, h5py, and the plotting dependencies used by the example notebooks.

cd ClearWater-modules
conda env create --file environment.yml --solver=libmamba
conda activate ClearWater-modules

The libmamba solver is substantially faster than the classic conda solver. If libmamba is not available, omit the --solver flag.

docs.title: 3. Install the Packages in Editable Mode
docs.text:
Install each of the three ClearWater packages in editable mode so that changes to the source code are reflected immediately without reinstallation:

pip install -e ../ClearWater-data
pip install -e ../ClearWater-riverine
pip install -e ../ClearWater-modules

The order matters because ClearWater-modules and ClearWater-riverine both depend on ClearWater-data. Install ClearWater-data first.

docs.title: 4. Verify the Installation
docs.text:
Activate the environment and confirm that each package imports cleanly:

conda activate ClearWater-modules
python -c "import clearwater_data; print(clearwater_data.__version__)"
python -c "import clearwater_riverine; print(clearwater_riverine.__version__)"
python -c "import clearwater_modules; print(clearwater_modules.__version__)"

Each command should print a version string. If any command raises ModuleNotFoundError, confirm that the pip install -e step completed successfully in the active conda environment.

To verify that the test suites run, execute pytest from each repository root:

cd ClearWater-modules
pytest

docs.title: Installation with pixi
docs.text: A pixi configuration is planned for ClearWater but is not yet available in the public repositories. Once published, pixi install from the repository root will create a reproducible environment without requiring a separate conda installation. Until then, use the conda workflow described above.

docs.title: Jupyter and Example Notebooks
docs.text:
The example notebooks in the examples/ directory of each repository depend on JupyterLab and several visualization libraries that are already included in the environment.yml. To launch JupyterLab:

conda activate ClearWater-modules
jupyter lab

The following JupyterLab extension is recommended for interactive development:

  • lckr-jupyterlab-variableinspector -- inspects live xarray and numpy objects.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Plots not displaying in notebooks

The ClearWater-riverine repository ships a fallback environment_working.yml that pins older versions of the visualization stack for cases where holoviews or hvplot figures fail to render. If plots do not appear after running a notebook cell, recreate the environment from environment_working.yml:

conda env create -f environment_working.yml --solver=libmamba

Fortran compiler requirements

ClearWater-Modules is pure Python and does not require a Fortran compiler. If a package fails to build with a Fortran-related error, confirm that pip is installing from the repository you cloned rather than from an older PyPI package with a similar name.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: ClearWater is a Python framework for coupled hydrodynamic and water quality modeling. The framework is designed around the idea that transport and reaction kinetics are separable concerns: a transport engine moves mass through a mesh, and a set of independent process modules compute the sources and sinks that modify constituent concentrations at each cell. This section describes the three packages that make up ClearWater, the Process-based architecture that governs how kinetics are computed, the chunked data layer that enables long simulations, and the HEC-RAS coupling that drives the transport grid.

docs.title: The Three Packages
docs.text:
ClearWater is distributed as three Python packages that are developed and versioned independently but are designed to be composed into a full simulation.

ClearWater-Riverine is a two-dimensional (2D) transport engine. ClearWater-Riverine reads HEC-RAS 2D HDF output, extracts the unstructured mesh geometry, face flows, cell volumes, and water surface elevations, and solves the advection-diffusion equation for an arbitrary number of constituents. ClearWater-Riverine assumes vertical homogeneity, so the model is best suited for riverine and estuarine systems where longitudinal and lateral gradients dominate over vertical stratification.

ClearWater-Modules provides the water quality reaction kinetics. The package contains the Temperature Simulation Module (TSM), the General Constituent Simulation Module (GSM), and the Nutrient Simulation Module (NSM1), along with a developing Nutrient Simulation Module II (NSM2). Each module computes the net reaction rate for its state variables at each mesh cell and time step; the resulting source/sink term is applied by the transport engine during integration.

ClearWater-Data is the data layer. ClearWater-Data provides a VariableRegistry abstraction that manages state variables across time and mesh dimensions, together with a ChunkedZarrDataStore that backs the registry with a zarr store on disk. This layer decouples the model state from Python process memory, which is the foundation for long-duration simulations.

docs.title: Process-Based Architecture
docs.text:
ClearWater is being refactored onto a unified Process abstract base class. Each kinetic module (temperature, floating algae, benthic algae, nitrogen, and so on) is implemented as a Process subclass that declares its required inputs, produced outputs, and configuration schema. The framework provides a ProcessFactory that instantiates processes from YAML configuration files, and a Model class that orchestrates the run.

Each Process has a three-phase lifecycle:

  1. init_process -- The process initializes its internal state, reads its configuration, and registers its variables with the VariableRegistry.
  2. run(time, registry) -- The process reads the current state from the registry, computes its kinetic source/sink terms, and writes updated values back to the registry at the specified time index.
  3. finalize_process -- The process releases resources and flushes any buffered output.

This design makes it possible to add new water quality processes without modifying the transport engine or the data layer, and it enforces explicit coupling between processes via the VariableRegistry rather than through shared Python objects.

docs.title: Chunked Zarr Data Layer
docs.text:
Long water quality simulations can produce output volumes that exceed available RAM, particularly when many constituents are simulated on fine meshes over multi-year periods. ClearWater addresses this through the ChunkedZarrDataStore, which stores simulation state as a chunked zarr array on disk. The VariableRegistry reads and writes state at a specific time index on demand via get_at_time() and set_at_time(), so only the currently active chunks are resident in memory.

This architecture enables out-of-core time stepping, where the model streams through a long simulation without holding the full time history in RAM, and it produces a self-describing xarray-compatible output dataset that can be analyzed incrementally.

docs.title: HEC-RAS Coupling
docs.text:
ClearWater-Riverine couples to HEC-RAS 2D as a post-processor on the HEC-RAS hydrodynamic solution. A typical workflow runs an unsteady HEC-RAS 2D simulation to produce a plan HDF file, then ClearWater-Riverine reads the HDF file to extract the mesh topology and the time series of face-averaged flows, cell volumes, and water surface elevations. ClearWater-Riverine then solves the transport equation on the HEC-RAS mesh using the HEC-RAS time step, and the ClearWater-Modules processes compute reaction kinetics at each step.

Because ClearWater reads HEC-RAS output rather than running inside HEC-RAS, users can leverage existing HEC-RAS 2D models of rivers, reservoirs, and floodplains for water quality studies without reconfiguring or re-running the hydrodynamic solution.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
This quickstart walks through a minimal coupled simulation that uses ClearWater-Riverine for 2D transport and the Temperature Simulation Module (TSM) from ClearWater-Modules for water temperature kinetics. The example assumes you have completed the Installation steps and have a HEC-RAS 2D plan HDF file available as input.

The full worked example, with all boundary condition inputs and plotting code, is available as a Jupyter notebook in the ClearWater-Riverine repository at examples/02_coupling_riverine_modules_tsm.ipynb. This page summarizes the essential steps.

docs.title: 1. Activate the Environment and Import Packages
docs.text:
Activate the conda environment created during installation and launch Python or JupyterLab:

conda activate ClearWater-modules
jupyter lab

In a new notebook or script, import the transport engine, the temperature module, and the data layer:

import xarray as xr
import pandas as pd
import clearwater_riverine as cwr
from clearwater_riverine.io import hdf
from clearwater_modules.tsm import EnergyBudget

docs.title: 2. Load the HEC-RAS Mesh and Flow Field
docs.text:
ClearWater-Riverine reads the mesh topology and the time series of cell volumes, face flows, and water surface elevations directly from a HEC-RAS 2D plan HDF file. Point the loader at your HEC-RAS plan file and specify the 2D flow area name:

ras_plan = "data/MyProject.p01.hdf"
flow_area = "MyFlowArea2D"

mesh = hdf.load_mesh(ras_plan, flow_area_name=flow_area)

The returned mesh is an xarray.Dataset that contains the unstructured grid geometry (cell centers, face connectivity, face areas) and the time-indexed hydrodynamic state.

docs.title: 3. Define Boundary and Initial Conditions
docs.text:
Provide boundary concentrations for the constituents you will simulate. For temperature, the boundaries are water temperature time series at each inflow. Load them from CSV files or construct them directly as pandas DataFrame objects:

initial_temperature = 15.0  # degrees C, applied uniformly across the mesh
boundary_conditions = pd.read_csv(
    "data/temperature_boundaries.csv",
    parse_dates=["datetime"],
).set_index("datetime")

The boundary file should contain one column per HEC-RAS boundary line, matching the names used in the HEC-RAS plan.

docs.title: 4. Configure the Temperature Process
docs.text:
Instantiate the TSM energy budget with the meteorological forcing required to close the surface heat balance (air temperature, dew point, wind speed, solar radiation, and cloud cover) and any site-specific parameters:

meteorology = xr.open_dataset("data/meteorology.nc")

temperature_process = EnergyBudget(
    meteorology=meteorology,
    wind_function_a=0.46,
    wind_function_b=9.2,
    sediment_heat_flux=True,
)

The EnergyBudget process computes net heat flux at each wetted cell on each time step and converts it to a temperature source term that is passed to the transport solver.

docs.title: 5. Run the Coupled Simulation
docs.text:
Create the coupled transport model, register the temperature process, and run the simulation over the HEC-RAS time window:

model = cwr.Transport(
    mesh=mesh,
    constituents={"temperature": initial_temperature},
    boundary_conditions={"temperature": boundary_conditions},
    diffusion_coefficient=0.1,  # m^2/s
)

model.register_process("temperature", temperature_process)

results = model.run(
    start_time=mesh.time.values[0],
    end_time=mesh.time.values[-1],
    output_path="output/tsm_quickstart.zarr",
)

Writing the output to a zarr store rather than a single NetCDF file enables memory-efficient streaming for long simulations. The ChunkedZarrDataStore writes one chunk per output interval, so only the currently active time slice is held in memory.

docs.title: 6. Inspect the Results
docs.text:
Open the output store as an xarray.Dataset and plot a time series at a cell of interest:

ds = xr.open_zarr("output/tsm_quickstart.zarr")

print(ds)
print(ds["temperature"].mean(dim="cell").to_pandas().head())

ds["temperature"].isel(cell=1250).plot()

The resulting xarray.Dataset contains the full simulated state (temperature, and any additional constituents you registered) on the original HEC-RAS mesh. Use standard xarray operations to compute spatial statistics, extract transects, or produce animations.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• Explore additional worked examples in the examples/ directory of each ClearWater repository.
  • Review the 01_getting_started_riverine.ipynb notebook in ClearWater-riverine/examples/ for a deeper discussion of the transport solver, boundary condition handling, and mass balance diagnostics.
  • Add the Nutrient Simulation Module (NSM1) to a coupled run by following examples/03_01_coupling_riverine_modules_nsm.ipynb.
  • Read the Overview for a conceptual description of the Process-based architecture and the chunked data layer.

docs.title: Release Notes
docs.text:
This page is under development.

This page will contain release notes for each version of the ClearWater framework, documenting new features, breaking changes, bug fixes, and upgrade instructions.

docs.title: Theory
docs.text: This section presents the theoretical foundations of the ClearWater framework. The pages here describe the governing equations, physical assumptions, and numerical techniques shared across the kinetic modules. Refer back to these pages from the module-specific user guide when you need the derivation or physical justification behind a particular rate or flux expression.

docs.title: In This Section
docs.text:
• Hydrodynamics summarizes the role of the external transport model and the scope of what ClearWater itself computes.
  • Temperature presents the surface energy balance used by TSM.
  • Kinetics documents the Arrhenius temperature correction, Monod / Michaelis-Menten limitation, stoichiometric ratios, and first-order decay formulations used across NSM1, GSM, CSM, and MSM.
  • Numerical Methods describes the explicit Euler time integration, positivity clipping, and chunked execution pattern.

docs.title: Hydrodynamics
docs.text: ClearWater is a water quality kinetics framework. It does not solve the shallow-water equations, the Navier-Stokes equations, or any hydrodynamic transport. Instead, ClearWater couples to an external hydrodynamic model that supplies velocity fields, depths, volumes, and transport fluxes at each time step. The kinetic modules (TSM, NSM1, GSM, CSM, MSM) then operate on each cell to compute the local source, sink, and reaction terms.

docs.title: Separation of Concerns
docs.text:
The ClearWater design separates two concerns that are often conflated in legacy water quality models:

  • Transport (advection, dispersion, exchange across cell faces) is handled by the hydrodynamic model.
  • Kinetics (biogeochemical reactions, heat fluxes, settling) is handled by the ClearWater modules.

Each time step, the hydrodynamic model transports the constituent fields; ClearWater then applies the cell-local kinetic tendencies. This operator-splitting approach is standard in coupled water quality modeling and keeps the kinetic modules independent of any particular hydrodynamic grid or solver.

docs.title: Supported Coupling: ClearWater-Riverine and HEC-RAS 2D
docs.text:
The current reference coupling is to HEC-RAS 2D through the ClearWater-Riverine package. In this configuration:

  • HEC-RAS 2D provides cell geometry, water depths, volumes, face velocities, and inter-cell transport fluxes from a pre-computed unsteady hydraulics run.
  • ClearWater-Riverine advances the transport of each tracked constituent on the 2D mesh at each time step.
  • TSM, NSM1, and the other modules compute the cell-local kinetic tendencies and update the state variables.

HEC-RAS 2D is run to completion first; ClearWater then reads the hydrodynamic output and advances water quality offline. This one-way coupling is appropriate for water quality studies because biogeochemistry does not affect the hydrodynamic solution at the scales of interest.

docs.title: Extending to Other Transport Models
docs.text: Because ClearWater modules interact with the transport solver only through the data registry (see ClearWater-Data), the same kinetic code can be coupled to other transport frameworks. Any model that can supply water depth, cell volume, water temperature forcing, and a time-stepping harness can drive ClearWater. Historical couplings include CE-QUAL-W2, GSSHA, and AdH in their original Fortran implementations.

docs.title: Practical Implications for Users
docs.text:
• Run the hydrodynamic model first and verify its outputs (depths, velocities, mass balance) before launching ClearWater.
  • Use the hydrodynamic time step, or a coarser multiple of it, as the ClearWater kinetic time step. Kinetic time steps finer than the hydrodynamic output resolution provide no additional accuracy.
  • Boundary conditions for water quality constituents (inflow concentrations, point loads) are applied through the transport model, not directly in the kinetic modules.

docs.title: Water Quality Kinetics
docs.text: Every reactive process in ClearWater is expressed as a cell-local rate that depends on water temperature, limiting resources, and stoichiometric conversion factors. This page describes the four kinetic formulations that recur throughout the ClearWater modules: Arrhenius temperature correction, Monod / Michaelis-Menten limitation, fixed stoichiometric ratios, and first-order decay.

docs.title: Arrhenius Temperature Correction
docs.text:
Biological and chemical rate constants depend strongly on water temperature. ClearWater applies the standard Arrhenius-form correction:

\[ r(T) = r_{20} \, \theta^{T - 20} \]

where:

  • \(r(T)\) is the rate constant at water temperature \(T\) (degrees C).
  • \(r_{20}\) is the rate constant at the reference temperature of 20 degrees C.
  • \(\theta\) is the dimensionless temperature coefficient (typically 1.02 to 1.10 for aquatic rate processes).

The value of \(\theta\) encodes how strongly a process responds to temperature. A value of 1.047 (common for many nitrification and mineralization rates) implies the rate roughly doubles for every 15 degrees C increase.

Warning

The Arrhenius formulation is extremely sensitive to unrealistic values of \(\theta\). A \(\theta\) of 999 would grow by many orders of magnitude per degree; a \(\theta\) of 0 would collapse the rate to zero everywhere except at 20 degrees C. Always verify \(\theta\) is a physically reasonable value (typically between 1.0 and 1.15) before running a simulation.

docs.title: Monod / Michaelis-Menten Limitation
docs.text:
When a process depends on a limiting substrate (for example, algal growth limited by nitrogen or phosphorus), ClearWater uses Monod kinetics:

\[ f(S) = \frac{S}{K_s + S} \]

where:

  • \(S\) is the substrate concentration.
  • \(K_s\) is the half-saturation constant; at \(S = K_s\) the limitation factor equals 0.5.

The limitation factor \(f(S)\) ranges from 0 (complete limitation) to 1 (no limitation). When multiple resources (for example, light, nitrogen, phosphorus) independently limit a process, the combined limitation may be taken as the minimum of the individual factors (Liebig's law) or as a multiplicative product, depending on the specific formulation.

docs.title: Inhibition
docs.text:
The same functional form is used with a sign change to represent inhibition by a solute. For example, nitrification is inhibited at low dissolved oxygen through:

\[ f_{\text{inhib}}(\text{DOX}) = \frac{\text{DOX}}{K_{\text{nit}} + \text{DOX}} \]

which approaches 0 at low oxygen and 1 at high oxygen.

docs.title: Stoichiometric Ratios
docs.text:
Reactions that convert between state variables (for example, algal growth converting NH4 into algal biomass) are governed by fixed stoichiometric ratios. NSM1 parameterizes algal stoichiometry as mass ratios of the form:

Parameter Description Default AWd Dry mass to chlorophyll-a 100 AWc Carbon to chlorophyll-a 40 AWn Nitrogen to chlorophyll-a 7.2 AWp Phosphorus to chlorophyll-a 1 AWa Oxygen to chlorophyll-a (photosynthesis) 1000

When the algal growth rate is applied, the same mass flux is subtracted from the nutrient pools in the ratios AWn : AWc : AWp and released to the dissolved oxygen pool in the ratio AWa. Benthic algae use an analogous set of ratios (BWd, BWc, BWn, BWp, BWa).

The Redfield ratio (C:N:P = 106:16:1 by moles) is the conceptual basis for these stoichiometric coefficients, but NSM1 exposes them as tunable parameters to support site-specific calibration.

docs.title: First-Order Decay
docs.text:
The simplest reactive formulation is first-order decay, used for CBOD oxidation, pathogen die-off, GSM generic constituents, and many hydrolysis and mineralization processes:

\[ \frac{\partial C}{\partial t} = -k(T) \, C \]

where \(k(T)\) is the Arrhenius-corrected rate constant (day\(^{-1}\)). The analytical solution in a closed system is exponential decay:

\[ C(t) = C_0 \, e^{-k(T) \, t} \]

First-order decay is an appropriate approximation when the decaying species is far below any saturating threshold for its consumer or catalyst.

docs.title: Combining the Formulations
docs.text:
NSM1 rate expressions typically combine all four elements. For example, the floating algal growth rate takes the form:

\[ \mu = \mu_{\max,20} \, \theta^{T-20} \, \min\left[ f_L, \frac{N}{K_{sN} + N}, \frac{P}{K_{sP} + P} \right] \]

and the nitrogen uptake rate is:

\[ \frac{\partial \text{NH4}}{\partial t} \bigg|_{\text{uptake}} = - \mu \, A_p \, \text{AWn} \cdot P_N \]

where \(P_N\) is the ammonia preference factor that partitions uptake between NH4 and NO3. This pattern (temperature-corrected maximum rate times minimum-of-limitations times stoichiometric conversion) recurs throughout the module.

docs.title: Related Pages
docs.text:
• NSM1 Overview for how these formulations combine into the full 13-variable nutrient model.
  • GSM Configuration for first-order decay applied to user-defined constituents.
  • Numerical Methods for the time integration scheme used to advance these rates.

docs.title: Numerical Methods
docs.text: ClearWater advances its kinetic state variables in time using explicit Euler integration, applies positivity clipping to prevent negative concentrations, and processes large grids in chunks that align with the ClearWater-Data storage backend. This page describes each of these techniques and the reasoning behind them.

docs.title: Explicit Euler Time Integration
docs.text:
Each state variable \(C\) is advanced from time \(t_n\) to \(t_{n+1} = t_n + \Delta t\) by:

\[ C_{n+1} = C_n + \Delta t \, \left. \frac{\partial C}{\partial t} \right|_n \]

where the right-hand-side tendency is evaluated entirely from quantities known at time \(t_n\). Explicit Euler is first-order accurate in time and requires no implicit solve. ClearWater uses this scheme for three reasons:

  • Simplicity. Each kinetic module computes a single tendency per variable per step. No linearization or Jacobian is required.
  • Vectorization. Every cell can be updated independently, which maps cleanly onto xarray and numpy array operations.
  • Interoperability. Operator splitting with the transport model is straightforward when both transport and kinetics use explicit schemes on the same time grid.

docs.title: Stability Considerations
docs.text:
Explicit Euler is conditionally stable. For a first-order decay process with rate \(k\), stability requires:

\[ \Delta t \leq \frac{2}{k} \]

For typical water quality rates (0.01 to 1 day\(^{-1}\)), this gives an upper bound of several hours to several days on \(\Delta t\). For the surface energy balance in TSM, the controlling time scale is the thermal response time of a shallow water column; a time step of one hour or less is typical.

Users who run into instability should first reduce the time step by a factor of two and rerun; if instability persists, inspect the parameter set for unphysically large rate constants.

docs.title: Positivity Clipping
docs.text:
Concentrations and temperatures are physical quantities with well-defined lower bounds. Explicit Euler can occasionally produce small negative values near zero (for example, when a depleting pool is pushed below zero by a large sink term). ClearWater applies a positivity clip after each update:

\[ C_{n+1} \leftarrow \max(C_{n+1}, C_{\min}) \]

where \(C_{\min}\) is either zero (for concentrations) or a small positive tolerance (for variables that appear in denominators). For water temperature, an upper bound is also applied.

Positivity clipping introduces a small mass non-conservation when activated, but for the magnitudes typically clipped (on the order of machine epsilon times the pool size) the effect on long-term mass balance is negligible. If clipping is invoked frequently on a variable, that is a signal that the time step is too large or that a parameter is driving the pool to zero too aggressively.

docs.title: Chunked Execution
docs.text:
Large simulations (high-resolution 2D grids times long time horizons) can easily produce state histories of tens to hundreds of gigabytes. ClearWater executes such simulations in chunks so that only a small portion of the state is in memory at any one time.
