The chunking pattern follows the zarr chunk shape declared in the data backend (see Zarr Data Store). A typical pattern is:

flowchart LR
    A[Start of time chunk] --> B[Read state at t_n from zarr]
    B --> C[Compute kinetic tendencies for all cells]
    C --> D[Update state to t_n+1]
    D --> E[Write state at t_n+1 to zarr]
    E --> F{More steps in chunk?}
    F -- Yes --> B
    F -- No --> G[Flush chunk to disk, release memory]
    G --> H[Next time chunk]

Within a chunk, all cells are updated in a single vectorized array operation. Between chunks, the backend flushes completed time slices to disk and reclaims the memory. Peak memory scales with chunk size, not with total simulation size.

docs.title: Operator Splitting with Transport
docs.text:
ClearWater uses first-order operator splitting between transport and kinetics. Within each time step, the transport model advects and disperses the state fields first, then the ClearWater modules apply the cell-local kinetic tendencies. This is sometimes called sequential splitting.

For the rates typical of water quality modeling, operator splitting error is small compared to the uncertainty in kinetic parameters and is usually acceptable. Higher-order splitting schemes (Strang splitting) could be substituted if greater accuracy were required, but the current implementation has found first-order splitting sufficient across all validated applications.

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text: Because ClearWater uses deterministic vectorized array operations, two runs with the same initial conditions, parameters, and forcing produce bit-identical results on the same hardware. This makes it straightforward to verify that a parameter change produced the intended effect and to diff output files during calibration.

docs.title: Temperature Theory
docs.text: The Temperature Simulation Module (TSM) applies conservation of energy to a well-mixed water column in each computational cell. This page presents the theoretical basis for the surface energy balance and the heat flux formulations used by TSM. For the specific equations and parameter settings implemented in the module, see the TSM Energy Balance page.

docs.title: Conservation of Energy
docs.text:
For a well-mixed water column of volume \(V\) and surface area \(A_s\), the first law of thermodynamics gives:

\[ \rho_w \, c_{p,w} \, V \, \frac{\partial T_w}{\partial t} = \sum_i q_i \, A_i \]

where the sum runs over all heat flux terms \(q_i\) (W m\(^{-2}\)) acting on the corresponding interfacial area \(A_i\). The density \(\rho_w\) and specific heat \(c_{p,w}\) of water are treated as constants because their variation over the range of natural water temperatures is small.

docs.title: Heat Flux Components
docs.text:
The total surface energy balance decomposes into five components at the air-water interface and one at the sediment-water interface:

\[ q_{\text{net}} = q_{sw} + q_{lw,in} - q_{lw,out} - q_{lat} - q_{sen} + \underbrace{q_{sed} \, (A_b / A_s)}_{\text{bed contribution}} \]

docs.title: Shortwave Radiation
docs.text: Incoming shortwave radiation is largely independent of water temperature and depends on solar geometry, atmospheric transmission, and cloud cover. A fraction \(\alpha_s\) (the surface albedo) is reflected; the remainder is absorbed in the water column. For a well-mixed column, all absorbed shortwave is treated as a surface heat flux.

docs.title: Longwave Radiation
docs.text: Both the atmosphere and the water surface radiate in the longwave band according to the Stefan-Boltzmann law, modified by an effective emissivity. The net longwave exchange is typically negative (net energy loss) at night and small but variable during the day. Cloud cover enhances downwelling longwave by reflecting water-emitted radiation back to the surface.

docs.title: Latent Heat (Evaporation)
docs.text: Evaporation removes latent heat from the water at a rate proportional to the vapor pressure deficit between the saturated air immediately above the water surface and the overlying atmosphere. The wind function \(f(U_w)\) encapsulates the turbulent transfer efficiency. Evaporation is usually the dominant cooling term in summer.

docs.title: Sensible Heat
docs.text: Sensible heat transfer is driven by the air-water temperature difference and shares the same wind function as evaporation (Bowen ratio analogy). Sensible heat can go in either direction; the water often loses sensible heat at night and gains it on cold-air days.

docs.title: Sediment Heat Flux
docs.text: Heat conducts across the sediment-water interface according to Fourier's law, driven by the temperature gradient between the water and the underlying bed. Sediment heat flux is usually small compared to surface fluxes in deep water but can be significant in shallow streams, where the bed acts as a thermal reservoir that moderates diel temperature swings.

docs.title: Sign Convention
docs.text: All fluxes are written so that positive values add energy to the water column. Loss terms (outgoing longwave, latent, sensible when \(T_w > T_a\)) appear with negative signs in the governing equation.

docs.title: Physical Assumptions
docs.text:
The TSM energy balance rests on the following standard assumptions:

  • The water column is well mixed vertically within each cell (no stratification).
  • Density and specific heat of water are constant over the simulated range.
  • Shortwave radiation is absorbed uniformly in the water column.
  • The surface is a free water surface; ice cover and under-ice processes are not represented explicitly.
  • Heat storage in the sediment is represented by a single active layer with prescribed thickness and temperature.

For stratified reservoirs, ice-covered waters, or systems where vertical temperature structure matters, a more detailed model (for example, CE-QUAL-W2) should be used upstream of ClearWater.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text: See the TSM Energy Balance page for the exact flux equations as implemented, and the TSM Configuration page for the parameters required to evaluate them.

docs.title: User Guide
docs.text:
This page is under development.

This section provides detailed documentation for each ClearWater component: ClearWater-Riverine (hydrodynamics), TSM (temperature), GSM (general constituent transport), NSM1 (nutrient simulation), and ClearWater-Data (data management).

docs.title: ClearWater-Data
docs.text: ClearWater-Data is the shared data-access layer used by the ClearWater water quality and temperature modules. It provides a single interface for reading, writing, and indexing the state variables and static parameters that flow between the transport model and each kinetics module.

docs.title: In This Section
docs.text:
• Overview describes the role of ClearWater-Data and the xarray-based architecture that supports both in-memory and chunked (zarr) workflows.
  • Variable Registry documents the VariableRegistry API for registering, looking up, and accessing state variables at specific time steps.
  • Zarr Data Store documents the ChunkedZarrDataStore for simulations that exceed memory or benefit from persistent, chunked I/O.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: ClearWater-Data is the shared data-access layer used across the ClearWater water quality framework. It decouples the kinetic modules (TSM, NSM1, GSM, CSM, MSM) from the storage backend so that the same module code runs against in-memory arrays, on-disk zarr stores, or spatially distributed fields supplied by a transport model. ClearWater-Data is built on xarray and numpy, which provide labeled multidimensional arrays with named dimensions for time, space, and variable.

docs.title: Design Goals
docs.text:
ClearWater-Data is designed to meet three requirements that recur across ClearWater simulations:

  • Uniform access. Every module reads and writes state variables through the same API, regardless of how the data are physically stored. This eliminates ad hoc per-module data plumbing.
  • Scale flexibility. Small simulations run entirely in memory with minimal overhead. Large simulations (long time series, high-resolution 2D grids, ensembles) can stream through a chunked zarr store without exhausting RAM.
  • Time-indexed history. Each state variable has an explicit time axis. Modules can request the value at the current time step, the previous time step, or any prior time, enabling multi-step integrators, diagnostics, and restart workflows.

docs.title: Core Components
docs.text:
Component Role VariableRegistry Central catalog of registered variables. Supports register, get_at_time, and set_at_time operations with dimension and type metadata. ChunkedZarrDataStore Disk-backed store that persists variables as chunked zarr arrays. Supports random access to time slices without loading the full history. In-memory backend Default backend that holds variables as xarray.DataArray objects in RAM. Used for short simulations and test fixtures.

Modules do not interact with the storage backend directly. They receive a registry, request variables by name, and write back updated values. The registry dispatches the underlying reads and writes to whichever backend is active.

docs.title: Variable Types
docs.text:
ClearWater-Data distinguishes three variable types that correspond to different update frequencies:

  • State variables are prognostic quantities integrated in time (for example, water temperature, NH4, DOX). They have a time dimension and are written at every step.
  • Dynamic variables are diagnostic or forcing fields that may change over time but are not integrated (for example, air temperature, wind speed, transport fluxes). They also carry a time dimension.
  • Static variables are parameters and coefficients that do not change during a simulation (for example, wind function coefficients, stoichiometric ratios). They are stored without a time dimension.

docs.title: Typical Workflow
docs.text:
A simulation using ClearWater-Data follows this pattern:

  1. Create a registry and choose a backend (in-memory or zarr).
  2. Register each state, dynamic, and static variable with its shape, dtype, and units.
  3. Initialize state variables at t = 0 using set_at_time.
  4. At each time step, the transport model and each kinetics module read and write variables through the registry.
  5. On completion, the registry is either discarded (in-memory) or closed to finalize the zarr store on disk.

docs.title: When to Use the Zarr Backend
docs.text:
The ChunkedZarrDataStore is the recommended backend when:

  • The simulation grid is large enough that holding the full history in memory is impractical.
  • Results must be persistent and accessible after the simulation completes.
  • Multiple processes or workflows need concurrent read access to the same simulation output.

For short tests, unit tests, or single-cell simulations, the in-memory backend is simpler and faster.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• See Variable Registry for the API used to register and access variables.
  • See Zarr Data Store for chunking strategy, memory footprint, and disk layout.

docs.title: Variable Registry
docs.text: The VariableRegistry is the central catalog that ClearWater modules use to read and write state, dynamic, and static variables. It provides a consistent API regardless of whether the underlying storage is an in-memory xarray.Dataset or a chunked zarr store on disk.

docs.title: Variable Types
docs.text:
The registry supports three variable types that correspond to different update behaviors.

Type Time Axis Mutable During Simulation Typical Examples State Yes Yes (integrated each step) T_water, NH4, DOX, Ap Dynamic Yes Yes (read from forcing or transport) T_air, U_wind, q_sw_inc Static No No Stoichiometric ratios, wind function coefficients, half-saturation constants

docs.title: Registering Variables
docs.text:
Each variable must be declared before it can be read or written. Registration fixes the variable's type, dimensions, data type, and units.

from clearwater_data import VariableRegistry

registry = VariableRegistry()

registry.register(
    name="T_water",
    kind="state",
    dims=("time", "cell"),
    dtype="float64",
    units="degC",
)

registry.register(
    name="k_20_NH4",
    kind="static",
    dims=("cell",),
    dtype="float64",
    units="1/day",
)

docs.title: Reading Variables at a Time Step
docs.text:
Use get_at_time to retrieve the value of a state or dynamic variable at a specific time index. Static variables are retrieved with get.

T_now = registry.get_at_time("T_water", t=step)
T_prev = registry.get_at_time("T_water", t=step - 1)
k20 = registry.get("k_20_NH4")

get_at_time returns an xarray.DataArray aligned to the spatial dimensions of the variable. The returned array may be a lazy dask-backed view when the zarr backend is active.

docs.title: Writing Variables at a Time Step
docs.text:
Use set_at_time to write a state or dynamic variable at a specific time index. The value being written must match the registered dimensions and dtype.

registry.set_at_time("T_water", t=step + 1, value=T_new)

Static variables are written once during initialization with set.

docs.title: Dimension and Type Checking
docs.text: The registry validates dimensions and dtypes on every read and write. Attempts to write a variable with mismatched shape or incompatible dtype raise an error before any data are stored. This catches shape bugs and unit errors early.

docs.title: Backend Selection
docs.text:
The registry dispatches reads and writes to whichever backend is active. To switch between in-memory and zarr storage, construct the registry with the appropriate backend:

# In-memory backend (default)
registry = VariableRegistry()

# Zarr-backed registry
from clearwater_data import ChunkedZarrDataStore
store = ChunkedZarrDataStore(path="./sim_output.zarr", chunks={"time": 24, "cell": 1000})
registry = VariableRegistry(backend=store)

See Zarr Data Store for details on chunking and disk layout.

docs.title: Typical Usage in a Time Step Loop
docs.text:
for step in range(n_steps):
    T_now = registry.get_at_time("T_water", t=step)
    T_air = registry.get_at_time("T_air", t=step)
    U = registry.get_at_time("U_wind", t=step)

    T_new = tsm_step(T_now, T_air, U, registry.get("a_wind"), ...)

    registry.set_at_time("T_water", t=step + 1, value=T_new)

docs.title: Summary of API
docs.text: Method Purpose register(name, kind, dims, dtype, units) Declare a new variable get(name) Retrieve a static variable set(name, value) Write a static variable get_at_time(name, t) Retrieve a state or dynamic variable at time index t set_at_time(name, t, value) Write a state or dynamic variable at time index t variables() List all registered variable names close() Flush and close the underlying backend (no-op for in-memory)

docs.title: Chunked Zarr Data Store
docs.text: The ChunkedZarrDataStore is the disk-backed storage backend for ClearWater-Data. It persists every registered variable as a chunked zarr array, which allows ClearWater to run simulations whose full state history does not fit in memory and to produce output that is readable by any tool in the xarray / zarr ecosystem.

docs.title: When to Use the Zarr Backend
docs.text:
Choose the zarr backend when one or more of the following conditions hold:

  • The simulation grid times the number of time steps exceeds available RAM.
  • Output must persist on disk for post-processing, visualization, or restart.
  • Multiple downstream tools (Jupyter notebooks, Dask workflows, external viewers) need random-access reads of the output.
  • Simulations run long enough that intermediate crashes would otherwise lose all results.

For short simulations, unit tests, or single-cell scenarios, the default in-memory backend is simpler.

docs.title: Storage Layout
docs.text:
Each registered variable becomes a zarr array under the store's root directory. The array dimensions match the variable's registered dimensions. Attributes such as units and long names are preserved in the zarr metadata.

A typical on-disk layout for a 2D simulation with state variables T_water and NH4 and forcing variable T_air looks like:

sim_output.zarr/
    T_water/
        .zarray
        .zattrs
        0.0, 0.1, ... (chunk files)
    NH4/
        ...
    T_air/
        ...
    .zgroup
    .zattrs

docs.title: Chunking Strategy
docs.text:
Chunks are the fundamental unit of I/O in zarr. Choosing chunk sizes well is the single most important tuning decision for the zarr backend.

General guidelines:

  • Align chunks with access patterns. ClearWater modules read and write one time slice per step across all cells. A chunk shape such as {"time": 24, "cell": N_cells} (one-day time chunks across the whole grid) works well when access is time-step-sequential.
  • Target 1--100 MB per chunk. Very small chunks generate excessive metadata overhead; very large chunks force loading more than needed.
  • Match chunk boundaries to analysis needs. If downstream analysis aggregates by day or by region, align the chunk boundaries so aggregations touch the minimum number of chunks.

Specify chunks when constructing the store:

from clearwater_data import ChunkedZarrDataStore

store = ChunkedZarrDataStore(
    path="./sim_output.zarr",
    chunks={"time": 24, "cell": 10000},
)

docs.title: Memory Footprint
docs.text:
The zarr backend holds only the active chunks in memory. When a module requests a time slice, the store loads the chunk containing that slice, returns a view, and releases the chunk when it is no longer referenced. Peak memory usage is therefore approximately:

\[ \text{Peak RAM} \approx \sum_{\text{variables}} \text{(chunk size)} \times \text{(active chunks per variable)} \]

For a grid of 100,000 cells, 8-byte floats, and a chunk shape of {"time": 24, "cell": 10000}, each chunk is \(24 \times 10{,}000 \times 8 = 1.9\) MB. A registry with 15 state variables touches roughly 30 MB when a single time slice is active, independent of the total number of time steps.

docs.title: Opening, Appending, and Reading
docs.text:
Create a new store by passing a path that does not yet exist. Re-open an existing store by passing the same path; the store detects the existing zarr group and attaches to it. Reads can proceed from any tool that understands zarr:

import xarray as xr

ds = xr.open_zarr("./sim_output.zarr")
print(ds)
T = ds["T_water"].sel(time=slice("2024-01-01", "2024-01-31"))

docs.title: Closing the Store
docs.text: Call store.close() (or registry.close() if you are working through the registry) when the simulation completes. This flushes any pending writes and finalizes the zarr metadata. Most zarr operations are write-through, so data loss from an unexpected crash is typically limited to the currently buffered chunk.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
• Write one full time slice per step rather than many small per-cell writes. The chunking strategy assumes contiguous spatial writes.
  • If the simulation is embarrassingly parallel across cells, ensure that parallel workers write to disjoint chunk regions to avoid contention.
  • For long simulations, periodically verify disk usage; zarr produces one small file per chunk, and file-system inode limits can become the binding constraint before disk space does.

docs.title: Related Pages
docs.text:
• Variable Registry for the API used to read and write variables.
  • Overview for the broader architecture of ClearWater-Data.

docs.title: General Constituents Simulation Module (GSM)
docs.text: The General Constituents Simulation Module (GSM) simulates arbitrary water quality constituents that follow first-order decay and optional settling. GSM is intended for conservative tracers, total dissolved solids, total suspended solids, simple organic compounds, and any user-defined constituent that does not require the specialized kinetics of NSM1, CSM, or MSM.

docs.title: In This Section
docs.text:
• Overview describes the GSM kinetic formulation and common use cases.
  • Configuration lists the parameters required to define one or more generic constituents.

docs.title: When to Use GSM
docs.text: Use GSM when a constituent can be adequately represented by first-order decay, temperature correction, and constant settling velocity. For nutrients, use NSM1. For contaminants with sorption and phase partitioning, use CSM. For mercury speciation, use MSM.

docs.title: GSM Configuration
docs.text: GSM is configured as a list of constituents. Each constituent has its own kinetic parameters and initial condition. The module supports an arbitrary number of constituents; they are integrated independently at each time step.

docs.title: Per-Constituent Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Units Description name string Constituent name used for output labeling units string Concentration units (for example, mg/L, ug/L, CFU/100mL) k_20 day\(^{-1}\) First-order decay rate at 20 degrees C. Set to 0 for a conservative constituent. theta dimensionless Arrhenius temperature coefficient. Typical values are 1.0 (no temperature dependence) to 1.08. v_s m day\(^{-1}\) Settling velocity. Set to 0 for a dissolved constituent. C0 same as units Initial concentration

docs.title: Temperature Correction
docs.text:
GSM applies the standard Arrhenius correction to the decay rate:

\[ k(T) = k_{20} \, \theta^{T - 20} \]

where \(T\) is the water temperature in degrees C at the current cell and time step. See the Kinetics theory page for background on the Arrhenius formulation.

docs.title: Settling
docs.text: The settling flux is applied as a loss term proportional to \(v_s / H\), where \(H\) is the cell water depth supplied by the transport model. The settled mass leaves the water column; GSM does not track it further. If resuspension or sediment-water coupling is required, use NSM1 or a specialized module.

docs.title: Example Configuration
docs.text:
The following example configures three constituents: a conservative tracer, total suspended solids with settling, and a temperature-dependent decaying organic compound.

gsm:
  constituents:
    - name: Tracer
      units: mg/L
      k_20: 0.0
      theta: 1.0
      v_s: 0.0
      C0: 1.0

    - name: TSS
      units: mg/L
      k_20: 0.0
      theta: 1.0
      v_s: 0.5
      C0: 50.0

    - name: Generic_Organic
      units: mg/L
      k_20: 0.1
      theta: 1.047
      v_s: 0.0
      C0: 10.0

docs.title: Initial Conditions
docs.text: Initial concentrations may be supplied as a scalar (applied uniformly across the grid) or as a spatial field matching the transport model grid.

docs.title: Boundary Conditions
docs.text: Boundary inflows for each GSM constituent must be supplied through the transport model. GSM does not impose boundary fluxes directly; it acts only on the cell-local state provided by the host model.

docs.title: Calibration Guidance
docs.text:
• For conservative tracers, verify that simulated concentrations match transport-only behavior before enabling decay or settling.
  • For first-order decay constituents, estimate \(k_{20}\) and \(\theta\) from laboratory incubations, literature values, or field calibration against observed concentrations.
  • For settling particulate constituents, \(v_s\) depends strongly on particle size distribution and flocculation behavior. Calibrate against observed deposition patterns or suspended sediment concentrations.

docs.title: Related Modules
docs.text:
• NSM1 for coupled nutrient and algae biogeochemistry.
  • See the Kinetics theory page for the general decay and temperature correction formulations used throughout ClearWater.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: The General Constituents Simulation Module (GSM) provides a lightweight kinetic framework for any number of user-defined water quality constituents. Each constituent is integrated independently using a first-order decay law with Arrhenius temperature correction and an optional settling flux. GSM is designed for substances that do not warrant the specialized biogeochemistry of the nutrient, contaminant, or mercury modules.

docs.title: What GSM Simulates
docs.text:
For each constituent \(C\), GSM integrates the cell-local budget:

\[ \frac{\partial C}{\partial t} = -k(T) \, C - \frac{v_s}{H} \, C \]

where:

  • \(C\) is the constituent concentration (user-defined units, for example mg L\(^{-1}\)).
  • \(k(T) = k_{20} \, \theta^{T-20}\) is the first-order decay rate at the current water temperature \(T\) (day\(^{-1}\)).
  • \(k_{20}\) is the decay rate at 20 degrees C.
  • \(\theta\) is the Arrhenius temperature coefficient.
  • \(v_s\) is the settling velocity (m day\(^{-1}\)).
  • \(H\) is the water column depth (m).

Setting \(k_{20} = 0\) and \(v_s = 0\) produces a fully conservative tracer. Setting only \(v_s = 0\) produces a dissolved reactive constituent. Setting only \(k_{20} = 0\) produces a settling particulate tracer.

docs.title: Typical Use Cases
docs.text: Constituent Type Decay Rate Settling Velocity Notes Conservative tracer (salinity, chloride, dye) 0 0 Advection and dispersion only; checks transport behavior Total suspended solids 0 > 0 Particulate tracer with gravitational settling Generic organic compound > 0 0 First-order biodegradation with temperature dependence Bacterial indicator > 0 0 Temperature-dependent die-off User-defined varies varies Any combination supported

docs.title: Module Scope
docs.text:
GSM computes only the cell-local kinetic tendencies. Advection, dispersion, and boundary fluxes are handled by the external transport model (for example, HEC-RAS 2D via ClearWater-Riverine). GSM receives the current concentration field and water temperature, computes the decay and settling tendencies, and returns the updated concentrations to the transport model.

Each constituent is integrated independently; GSM does not represent reactions between constituents. If coupling between species is required, use the appropriate specialized module or extend GSM with custom kinetics.

docs.title: Inputs at a Glance
docs.text: Category Examples Constituent properties Decay rate at 20 degrees C, Arrhenius coefficient, settling velocity Environmental drivers Water temperature, water depth Initial conditions Initial concentration for each constituent

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text: GSM produces an updated concentration field for each configured constituent at every time step. Decay and settling fluxes are available as diagnostic outputs for mass balance verification.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text: See the Configuration page for the full list of parameters and an example configuration for multiple constituents.

docs.title: Nutrient Simulation Module v1 (NSM1)
docs.text: The Nutrient Simulation Module v1 (NSM1) simulates the coupled cycling of nitrogen, phosphorus, carbon, dissolved oxygen, algae, pathogens, alkalinity, particulate organic matter, and carbonaceous biochemical oxygen demand (CBOD) in surface waters. NSM1 is the primary water quality kinetics engine of ClearWater.

docs.title: In This Section
docs.text:
• Overview describes the 13 state variables, their interactions, and the coupling structure that drives the module.
  • State-variable reference pages (floating algae, benthic algae, nitrogen, phosphorus, carbon, CBOD, dissolved oxygen, pathogens, alkalinity) document the rate equations, parameters, and default values for each group.

docs.title: Related Theory
docs.text: See the Kinetics page for the general formulations (Arrhenius correction, Monod limitation, stoichiometric ratios) used throughout NSM1.

docs.title: Alkalinity
docs.text:
This page is under development.

Documents the alkalinity process, corresponding to dAlkdt in v1 nsm1/processes.py. This page will cover how alkalinity is affected by nitrification, denitrification, algal uptake, and carbon dioxide exchange, and its role in buffering pH in the water column.

docs.title: Benthic Algae
docs.text:
This page is under development.

Documents the benthic algae (periphyton) process, corresponding to dAbdt in v1 nsm1/processes.py. This page will cover benthic algal growth, respiration, density-dependent limitations, and the influence of benthic algae on nutrient uptake and dissolved oxygen at the sediment-water interface.

docs.title: Carbon
docs.text:
This page is under development.

Documents the carbon processes, corresponding to dPOCdt, dDOCdt, and dDICdt in v1 nsm1/processes.py. This page will cover particulate organic carbon (POC) dissolution and settling, dissolved organic carbon (DOC) oxidation, and dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) dynamics including CO2 exchange and alkalinity coupling.

docs.title: Carbonaceous BOD
docs.text:
This page is under development.

Documents the carbonaceous biochemical oxygen demand (CBOD) process, corresponding to dCBODdt in v1 nsm1/processes.py. This page will cover CBOD oxidation kinetics, settling, and the CBOD contribution to dissolved oxygen consumption.

docs.title: Dissolved Oxygen
docs.text:
This page is under development.

Documents the dissolved oxygen (DOX) budget, corresponding to dDOXdt in v1 nsm1/processes.py. This page will detail the nine source/sink terms in the DO balance: atmospheric reaeration, photosynthesis, respiration, nitrification, CBOD oxidation, sediment oxygen demand (SOD), and carbon oxidation, along with the Arrhenius temperature corrections applied to each rate.

docs.title: Floating Algae
docs.text:
This page is under development.

Documents the floating algae (phytoplankton) process, corresponding to dApdt in v1 nsm1/processes.py. This page will cover algal growth (light- and nutrient-limited), respiration, settling, and the effects of floating algae on dissolved oxygen, nitrogen, and phosphorus cycling.

docs.title: Nitrogen Cycle
docs.text:
This page is under development.

Documents the nitrogen cycle processes, corresponding to dOrgNdt, dNH4dt, and dNO3dt in v1 nsm1/processes.py. This page will cover organic nitrogen hydrolysis, ammonia nitrification, nitrate denitrification, algal uptake and release, atmospheric deposition, and sediment fluxes for each nitrogen species.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: The Nutrient Simulation Module v1 (NSM1) simulates the coupled biogeochemical cycling of nutrients, organic matter, oxygen, and associated constituents in surface waters. NSM1 represents the processes that drive eutrophication, dissolved oxygen dynamics, and carbon and nutrient fate in rivers, reservoirs, and estuaries. The module is a modernized Python port of the ERDC Fortran NSM-I code (Zhang and Johnson, 2016).

docs.title: State Variables
docs.text: NSM1 integrates 13 prognostic state variables, organized into six conceptual groups.

docs.title: Algae
docs.text: Variable Symbol Units Description Floating algae Ap ug-Chla L\(^{-1}\) Phytoplankton biomass as chlorophyll-a Benthic algae Ab g D m\(^{-2}\) Attached benthic algal biomass, areal density

docs.title: Nitrogen
docs.text: Variable Symbol Units Description Organic nitrogen OrgN mg-N L\(^{-1}\) Dissolved and particulate organic N Ammonia nitrogen NH4 mg-N L\(^{-1}\) Ammonium plus ammonia Nitrate nitrogen NO3 mg-N L\(^{-1}\) Nitrate plus nitrite

docs.title: Phosphorus
docs.text: Variable Symbol Units Description Organic phosphorus OrgP mg-P L\(^{-1}\) Dissolved and particulate organic P Total inorganic phosphorus TIP mg-P L\(^{-1}\) Orthophosphate and sorbed inorganic P

docs.title: Carbon
docs.text: Variable Symbol Units Description Particulate organic carbon POC mg-C L\(^{-1}\) Non-algal particulate organic C Dissolved organic carbon DOC mg-C L\(^{-1}\) Dissolved organic C Dissolved inorganic carbon DIC mg-C L\(^{-1}\) CO\(_2\), HCO\(_3^-\), and CO\(_3^{2-}\)

docs.title: Oxygen and Oxygen Demand
docs.text: Variable Symbol Units Description Dissolved oxygen DOX mg-O\(_2\) L\(^{-1}\) Dissolved oxygen concentration CBOD CBOD mg-O\(_2\) L\(^{-1}\) Carbonaceous biochemical oxygen demand (one or more groups)

docs.title: Other
docs.text: Variable Symbol Units Description Pathogens PX CFU 100mL\(^{-1}\) Generic pathogen indicator Alkalinity Alk mg-CaCO\(_3\) L\(^{-1}\) Total alkalinity Particulate organic matter POM mg L\(^{-1}\) Non-algal particulate organic matter

docs.title: How the State Variables Couple
docs.text:
NSM1 state variables are coupled through growth, respiration, nitrification, denitrification, hydrolysis, mineralization, oxidation, settling, and reaeration. Figure 1 shows the dominant mass transfers between groups.

flowchart LR
    subgraph Nitrogen
        OrgN --> NH4
        NH4 --> NO3
        NO3 -->|denitrification| N2[N2 gas]
    end

    subgraph Phosphorus
        OrgP --> TIP
    end

    subgraph Carbon
        POC --> DOC
        DOC --> DIC
        DIC <-->|reaeration| Atm1[Atmosphere]
    end

    Algae[Floating Algae Ap] -->|death| OrgN
    Algae -->|death| OrgP
    Algae -->|death| POC
    Algae -->|respiration| NH4
    Algae -->|respiration| TIP
    Algae -->|respiration| DIC
    Algae -->|photosynthesis| DOX
    NH4 -->|uptake| Algae
    NO3 -->|uptake| Algae
    TIP -->|uptake| Algae

    BAlgae[Benthic Algae Ab] -.->|death/resp| OrgN
    BAlgae -.->|death/resp| OrgP
    BAlgae -.->|photosynthesis| DOX

    NH4 -->|nitrification| DOX_sink[DOX consumption]
    CBOD -->|oxidation| DOX_sink
    DOC -->|oxidation| DOX_sink
    DOX <-->|reaeration| Atm2[Atmosphere]

    POM --> Settling[Settling / burial]
    POC --> Settling

Key coupling behaviors include:

  • Algal growth consumes NH4, NO3, TIP, and DIC in fixed stoichiometric ratios (AWc, AWn, AWp, AWa) and releases DOX. Growth is limited by the minimum of light, nitrogen, and phosphorus availability through Monod half-saturation kinetics.
  • Algal death and respiration return organic matter to OrgN, OrgP, and POC, and inorganic forms to NH4, TIP, and DIC.
  • Nitrification oxidizes NH4 to NO3, consuming DOX. The nitrification rate is suppressed at low oxygen through a Monod inhibition term.
  • Denitrification reduces NO3 to N\(_2\) gas under low-oxygen conditions, providing an anaerobic nitrogen sink.
  • Organic matter mineralization converts OrgN, OrgP, POC, and DOC to inorganic forms through first-order hydrolysis and oxidation reactions that consume DOX.
  • Reaeration exchanges DOX and DIC with the atmosphere at the air-water interface based on gas transfer velocities.
  • Alkalinity is modified by nitrification, denitrification, algal uptake, and photosynthesis based on the stoichiometric coefficients r_alkaa, r_alkan, r_alkn, r_alkden, r_alkba, and r_alkbn.
  • Settling removes particulate constituents (Ap, OrgN, OrgP, POC, POM, sorbed TIP) from the water column at user-specified velocities.
  • CBOD represents oxidizable organic matter not already tracked through DOC or POC; it is oxidized by first-order kinetics and consumes DOX.
  • Pathogens decay by first-order kinetics with temperature dependence.

docs.title: Temperature Dependence
docs.text:
Every rate constant in NSM1 is corrected to the current water temperature using the Arrhenius formulation:

\[ r(T) = r_{20} \, \theta^{T - 20} \]

See the Kinetics theory page for details.

docs.title: Inputs and Outputs
docs.text: NSM1 requires water temperature (typically supplied by TSM), water depth, and for algal growth, photosynthetically active radiation. Initial conditions are required for each enabled state variable. NSM1 produces updated concentration fields at each time step and reports component rate terms (uptake, respiration, nitrification, mineralization, etc.) as diagnostic outputs.

docs.title: Module Configuration
docs.text:
NSM1 groups its parameters into sets that correspond to each state variable group: algae, benthic algae, nitrogen, phosphorus, carbon, CBOD, dissolved oxygen, pathogens, alkalinity, POM, and N2. Defaults for each group are provided in the code, but users should review and adjust them for site-specific applications.

Warning

Some default parameters in NSM1 use sentinel placeholder values that must be overridden before running the model (for example, settling velocities, reaeration coefficients, and sediment oxygen demand). Verify that your configuration supplies realistic values for every rate and coefficient, not only the ones you intend to tune.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text: Refer to the individual state-variable pages in this section for the rate equations, parameter tables, and default values used for each group.

docs.title: Pathogen Kinetics
docs.text:
This page is under development.

Documents the pathogen fate and transport process, corresponding to dPathogensdt in v1 nsm1/processes.py. This page will cover first-order pathogen die-off kinetics, including temperature-dependent decay, settling, and light inactivation.

docs.title: Phosphorus
docs.text:
This page is under development.

Documents the phosphorus processes, corresponding to dOrgPdt and dTIPdt in v1 nsm1/processes.py. This page will cover organic phosphorus mineralization, total inorganic phosphorus (TIP) dynamics including algal uptake and release, settling, and sediment phosphorus flux.

docs.title: ClearWater-Riverine
docs.text: ClearWater-Riverine is a two-dimensional (2D), depth-averaged water quality transport framework. The framework reads hydrodynamic output from HEC-RAS 2D and solves the advection-diffusion equation for one or more constituents on the same unstructured mesh used by HEC-RAS. ClearWater-Riverine couples with the ClearWater Modules (Temperature Simulation Module, Nutrient Simulation Module) to add source and sink terms to the transported constituents.

docs.title: Section Contents
docs.text:
• Overview -- framework concepts, relationship to HEC-RAS, mesh structure, and coupling with ClearWater Modules.
  • Configuration -- YAML configuration reference for constituents, initial conditions, boundary conditions, and diffusion.
  • Boundary Conditions -- boundary condition types, the boundary condition CSV format, and time interpolation behavior.
  • Transport Solver -- finite volume discretization, implicit time stepping, sparse linear solve, and the per-timestep update loop.
  • Post-Processing -- mass balance checks, mass flux recovery, edge vertical area, and volume accounting.
  • Plotting -- static plots, interactive dynamic maps, and scatter-based quick plots.

docs.title: Where to Start
docs.text: If you are new to ClearWater-Riverine, read the Overview first. Users preparing a simulation should move on to Configuration and Boundary Conditions. Users interpreting results should consult Post-Processing and Plotting.

docs.title: Boundary Conditions
docs.text: ClearWater-Riverine applies constituent boundary conditions at the HEC-RAS 2D boundary lines that appear in the hydrodynamic plan file. Each boundary line carries a user-supplied time series of concentration values that the framework aligns with the model time axis, interpolates, and injects at the associated boundary faces. This page documents the initial condition and boundary condition CSV formats, the time alignment behavior, and the handling of inflow versus outflow faces.

docs.title: Initial Conditions
docs.text: Initial conditions are specified per constituent in a CSV file. The file lists the starting concentration for each cell in the domain at the first model timestep.

docs.title: File Format
docs.text:
The initial condition CSV requires two columns.

Column Type Description Cell_Index integer Cell index (nface) in the ClearWater-Riverine mesh. Must correspond to the zero-based cell indexing used by the HEC-RAS 2D mesh. Concentration float Initial concentration for the cell in the units declared in the configuration.

Cells that are not listed in the CSV file are initialized to zero. The loader casts Cell_Index to an integer.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Cell_Index,Concentration
0,0.0
1,0.0
1250,10000.0
1251,10000.0

The loader for initial conditions is implemented in Constituent.set_initial_conditions in src/clearwater_riverine/constituents.py.

docs.title: Boundary Conditions
docs.text: Boundary conditions are specified per constituent in a CSV file. The file lists time-varying concentration values for each HEC-RAS boundary line.

docs.title: File Format
docs.text:
The boundary condition CSV requires three columns.

Column Type Description RAS2D_TS_Name string Name of the HEC-RAS 2D boundary line, exactly as it appears in the HEC-RAS plan. Datetime datetime Timestamp for the entry. Any format recognized by pandas.to_datetime is accepted. Concentration float Constituent concentration at the boundary line at the given time, in the units declared in the configuration.

ClearWater-Riverine groups rows by RAS2D_TS_Name and aligns each group with the model time axis using pandas.merge_asof followed by linear interpolation.

docs.title: Time Alignment and Interpolation
docs.text:
ClearWater-Riverine aligns the user-supplied boundary time series with the HEC-RAS output time axis in two steps.

  1. Backward-fill alignment. pandas.merge_asof joins the user time series to the model time axis by pairing each model timestamp with the most recent prior user timestamp. This behaves as a forward-fill from the user perspective: a user value at 02:00 applies to every model timestep from 02:00 until the next user entry. Model timesteps earlier than the first user entry receive NaN.
  2. Linear interpolation. pandas.DataFrame.interpolate(method='linear') fills interior NaN values by linearly interpolating across the aligned time series. This smooths abrupt transitions when the user time series is sparser than the model time axis.

The practical effect is that dense user time series (one entry per model timestep) are passed through unchanged, while sparse user time series are linearly interpolated between the provided entries. Leading NaN values (times before the first user entry) remain NaN and are treated as zero at the boundary.

Note

If you need true step (forward-fill) behavior rather than linear interpolation, supply the time series at the full model resolution with repeated values.

docs.title: Inflow Versus Outflow Behavior
docs.text:
The direction of flow at a boundary face determines how ClearWater-Riverine applies the boundary concentration.

  • Inflow faces. When the HEC-RAS face flow is directed into the domain, ClearWater-Riverine uses the user-supplied boundary concentration as the upstream value for the upwind advection term. Mass enters the domain at the specified concentration.
  • Outflow faces. When the HEC-RAS face flow is directed out of the domain, the upwind advection term uses the interior cell concentration. The user-supplied boundary concentration has no effect on outflow. This is equivalent to a zero-gradient (Neumann) outflow condition for the transported constituent.

Because the inflow and outflow behavior is determined by the sign of the HEC-RAS face flow at each timestep, tidal and reversing boundaries are handled automatically.

docs.title: Mapping Boundary Lines to Faces
docs.text: ClearWater-Riverine reads the boundary condition line dataset from the HEC-RAS plan HDF file to determine which faces belong to each boundary line. The framework stores this mapping in simulation.boundary_data, a pandas.DataFrame with at least the columns Name, BC Line ID, and Face Index. Post-processing utilities use this mapping to compute per-boundary mass fluxes; see Post-Processing.

docs.title: Boundary Condition Coverage
docs.text: The boundary condition CSV does not need to cover every boundary line defined in the HEC-RAS plan. Boundary lines that are absent from the CSV receive a concentration of zero at every timestep. This is appropriate for clean-water inflows and for outflow boundaries where the user-supplied concentration is ignored.

docs.title: Validation Tips
docs.text:
• Confirm that RAS2D_TS_Name values in the CSV match the boundary line names in the HEC-RAS plan exactly, including spaces and capitalization.
  • Confirm that Cell_Index values in the initial condition CSV fall within the range [0, nreal) where nreal is the number of real cells in the mesh.
  • If concentrations at an inflow appear as NaN during the early part of the simulation, extend the boundary condition CSV backward in time so that the first user entry occurs at or before the simulation start time.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: ClearWater-Riverine reads model setup from a YAML configuration file. The configuration file points to the HEC-RAS 2D flow field, sets the diffusion coefficient, and defines each transported constituent with its initial and boundary conditions. This page documents the configuration schema, provides a complete example, and explains how to pass the configuration to the ClearwaterRiverine class.

docs.title: Top-Level Schema
docs.text:
The configuration file uses three required top-level keys. ClearWater-Riverine raises a ValueError if any required key is missing.

Key Type Description flow_field_filepath string Path to the HEC-RAS 2D plan HDF5 file (for example, OhioRiver_m.p22.hdf). diffusion_coefficient float Scalar diffusion coefficient applied over the entire domain. Units depend on the HEC-RAS project (m^2 s^-1 for metric, ft^2 s^-1 for imperial). constituents mapping Dictionary of constituent definitions. Each key is the constituent name used throughout the simulation.

docs.title: Constituent Schema
docs.text:
Each entry under constituents is a mapping with the following required keys.

Key Type Description initial_conditions string Path to a CSV file that specifies initial concentrations by cell index. boundary_conditions string Path to a CSV file that specifies time-varying boundary concentrations for each HEC-RAS boundary line. units string Units string stored on the constituent data array (for example, mg/L, CFU/100mL, degC). The value is attached as an attribute and used in plots.

ClearWater-Riverine validates that every constituent carries initial_conditions and boundary_conditions. A missing key raises a ValueError that identifies both the missing field and the constituent.

docs.title: Example Configuration
docs.text:
The following configuration defines a two-constituent simulation with temperature and E. coli.

flow_field_filepath: data/ohio_river/OhioRiver_m.p22.hdf
diffusion_coefficient: 10.0

constituents:
  temperature:
    initial_conditions: data/ohio_river/temperature_initial.csv
    boundary_conditions: data/ohio_river/temperature_boundary.csv
    units: degC
  ecoli:
    initial_conditions: data/ohio_river/ecoli_initial.csv
    boundary_conditions: data/ohio_river/ecoli_boundary.csv
    units: CFU/100mL

See Boundary Conditions for the CSV file formats referenced by initial_conditions and boundary_conditions.

docs.title: Loading a Configuration
docs.text:
You can drive a simulation directly from a configuration file by passing config_filepath to the ClearwaterRiverine constructor.

from clearwater_riverine import ClearwaterRiverine

simulation = ClearwaterRiverine(
    config_filepath="configs/ohio_river.yml",
    verbose=True,
)

for _ in range(len(simulation.mesh.time) - 1):
    simulation.update()

simulation.finalize(save=True, output_filepath="results/ohio_river.zarr")

When config_filepath is provided, ClearWater-Riverine reads the YAML file, validates required keys, loads the HEC-RAS mesh from flow_field_filepath, and builds a Constituent object for each entry under constituents.

docs.title: Overriding Configuration Fields at Runtime
docs.text:
The ClearwaterRiverine constructor accepts several keyword arguments that override or replace configuration fields.

Argument Effect flow_field_file_path Overrides flow_field_filepath from the YAML configuration. Required if no config_filepath is provided. diffusion_coefficient_input Overrides diffusion_coefficient from the YAML configuration. constituent_dict Replaces the constituents mapping. Use this when constructing a model programmatically without a YAML file. datetime_range Limits the simulation to a subset of HEC-RAS output times. Accepts a tuple of integer indices or ISO datetime strings. mesh_file_path Loads a previously saved ClearWater-Riverine mesh (Zarr) instead of reading HEC-RAS output. Post-processing and plotting are supported in this mode; new simulations are not. verbose Prints progress messages during mesh loading and parameter calculation.

docs.title: Programmatic Configuration
docs.text:
When a YAML file is not convenient, you can supply the constituent configuration directly as a Python dictionary.

from clearwater_riverine import ClearwaterRiverine

constituent_dict = {
    "ecoli": {
        "initial_conditions": "data/ecoli_initial.csv",
        "boundary_conditions": "data/ecoli_boundary.csv",
        "units": "CFU/100mL",
    },
}

simulation = ClearwaterRiverine(
    flow_field_file_path="data/OhioRiver_m.p22.hdf",
    diffusion_coefficient_input=10.0,
    constituent_dict=constituent_dict,
    verbose=True,
)

Note

The programmatic form mirrors the YAML schema exactly. Each constituent dictionary must include initial_conditions, boundary_conditions, and units.

docs.title: Validation Errors
docs.text:
ClearWater-Riverine raises descriptive errors when the configuration is incomplete.

  • Missing top-level key: Missing ['diffusion_coefficient'] from configuration file.
  • Missing constituent key: Missing initial_conditions from ecoli in the model config.
  • Missing hydrodynamic source and programmatic inputs: Missing a 'config_filepath' or a 'constituent_dict' and 'flow_field_file_path' to run the model.

Address the reported field and rerun. The configuration parser is implemented in src/clearwater_riverine/io/config.py.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: ClearWater-Riverine is a modern, Python-based water quality transport framework developed by the U.S. Army Engineer Research and Development Center (ERDC), Environmental Laboratory (EL). The framework solves the two-dimensional, depth-averaged advection-diffusion equation on the unstructured mesh produced by an HEC-RAS 2D hydrodynamic run. ClearWater-Riverine consumes the HEC-RAS flow field rather than solving for flow itself, which lets modelers reuse calibrated HEC-RAS projects for water quality analysis without duplicating the hydrodynamic effort.

docs.title: What ClearWater-Riverine Does
docs.text:
ClearWater-Riverine computes the transport of one or more scalar constituents through a river, floodplain, estuary, or shallow lake represented by an HEC-RAS 2D mesh. For each constituent, the framework:

  • Advances a concentration field through time using the flow field (face velocities, face flows, cell volumes, and water surface elevations) from HEC-RAS.
  • Applies advection along cell faces using an upwind finite volume scheme.
  • Applies diffusion across cell faces using a user-specified diffusion coefficient.
  • Applies boundary condition concentrations at inflow faces and zero-gradient behavior at outflow faces.
  • Records advective, diffusive, and total mass flux across every edge for post-processing.

The framework handles multiple constituents simultaneously by sharing a single hydrodynamic mesh and a single left-hand side matrix per timestep. Each constituent carries its own initial conditions, boundary conditions, and right-hand side vector.

docs.title: Relationship to HEC-RAS
docs.text:
ClearWater-Riverine reads an HEC-RAS 2D plan HDF5 file (typically named *.pNN.hdf) and extracts:

  • 2D Flow Area geometry, including node coordinates, cell centers, face-node connectivity, and cell-edge connectivity.
  • Time-varying face flows and face velocities.
  • Time-varying water surface elevations and derived cell volumes.
  • Boundary condition line definitions, including the faces associated with each boundary line.

The HEC-RAS hydrodynamic solution is the source of truth for flow. ClearWater-Riverine does not modify flow, depth, or volume; the framework consumes these values as inputs to the transport equation. As a result, the temporal resolution and spatial resolution of transport are dictated by the HEC-RAS output.

docs.title: Mesh Concepts
docs.text:
The computational mesh follows the UGRID conventions for unstructured grids and is represented as an xarray.Dataset. The principal dimensions and variables include:

  • nface -- the cell (face) dimension; each entry corresponds to one 2D cell.
  • nedge -- the edge dimension; each entry corresponds to one face between two cells or between a cell and a boundary.
  • time -- the time dimension from the HEC-RAS output.
  • nreal -- the number of real (interior) cells, stored as an attribute. Ghost cells, which represent boundary inflows and outflows, are indexed after the real cells.

Each constituent is stored as a (time, nface) data array on the mesh. Advection coefficients, diffusion coefficients, face flows, volumes, and mass flux arrays are stored on either (time, nface) or (time, nedge) dimensions as appropriate.

docs.title: Time Integration
docs.text:
ClearWater-Riverine advances the solution using an implicit finite volume scheme. At each timestep the framework:

  1. Assembles a sparse left-hand side matrix A of size (nreal + 1, nreal + 1) from advection and diffusion coefficients.
  2. Assembles a right-hand side vector b for each constituent that incorporates the previous timestep concentrations, boundary condition inflows, and volume changes.
  3. Solves the sparse linear system A x = b using scipy.sparse.linalg.spsolve.
  4. Writes the updated concentration into the mesh and records advective, diffusive, and total mass flux on each edge.

The left-hand side matrix depends only on flow and geometry, so ClearWater-Riverine assembles it once per timestep and reuses it across all constituents. See the Transport Solver page for details.

docs.title: Coupling with ClearWater Modules
docs.text:
ClearWater-Riverine is the transport layer beneath the ClearWater water quality modules. A coupled simulation applies the modules as source and sink terms between transport timesteps:

  1. ClearWater-Riverine advances all transported state variables one timestep.
  2. The host script extracts the updated state from the Riverine mesh and passes it to a ClearWater module (for example, the Temperature Simulation Module or the Nutrient Simulation Module).
  3. The module computes reaction and exchange rates (for example, surface heat exchange, nitrification, algal growth, reaeration) and returns updated concentrations.
  4. The host script pushes the updated concentrations back into the Riverine mesh via the update method with an update_concentration dictionary.
  5. The loop repeats until the end of the simulation horizon.

This operator-splitting pattern separates transport from kinetics and lets you swap modules without modifying the transport framework. Example coupled workflows are provided in the examples/ directory of the ClearWater-riverine repository, including basic transport (01_getting_started_riverine.ipynb), TSM coupling (02_coupling_riverine_modules_tsm.ipynb), and NSM coupling (03_01_coupling_riverine_modules_nsm.ipynb).

docs.title: Typical Applications
docs.text:
ClearWater-Riverine is well suited to:

  • Conservative tracer transport, such as dye studies and travel-time analysis.
  • Pathogen transport with first-order decay, such as the Ohio River E. coli case study.
  • Thermal discharge studies when coupled with the Temperature Simulation Module.
  • Nutrient and dissolved oxygen modeling when coupled with the Nutrient Simulation Module.
  • Emergency response screening for spills in riverine systems.

The framework assumes vertical homogeneity and is therefore not appropriate for strongly stratified systems. For stratified reservoirs, use a laterally averaged 2D or fully 3D model.

docs.title: Assumptions and Limitations
docs.text:
• ClearWater-Riverine assumes depth-averaged conditions. The framework does not resolve vertical gradients.
  • ClearWater-Riverine requires a valid HEC-RAS 2D plan HDF file as the hydrodynamic driver when initializing a new simulation. Post-processing and plotting workflows can operate on a previously saved ClearWater-Riverine mesh without the original HEC-RAS file.
  • The diffusion coefficient is currently specified as a single scalar applied to the entire domain. Spatially variable diffusion is not exposed through the standard configuration.
  • Hotstart (restart from a previously saved simulation) is not currently supported.

docs.title: Plotting
docs.text: ClearWater-Riverine provides built-in plotting utilities that render constituent concentration fields on the HEC-RAS 2D mesh. The plotting methods are attached to the ClearwaterRiverine class and use matplotlib, HoloViews, and GeoViews to produce both static images and interactive dynamic maps. This page documents each plotting method and shows how to use them in a Jupyter notebook.

docs.title: Plotting Methods Overview
docs.text:
Method Output Backend Typical Use static_plot Single static image at one timestep matplotlib + geopandas Publication figures and snapshots at a specific time. plot Interactive dynamic map with a time slider GeoViews + HoloViews Exploratory review of simulation evolution with basemap. quick_plot Interactive scatter plot of cell centroids HoloViews Fast visual diagnostic during model development.

All three methods accept a constituent_name argument. When constituent_name is omitted, ClearWater-Riverine plots the first constituent in the model and issues a warning.

docs.title: Static Plot
docs.text: The static_plot method produces a matplotlib figure of cell polygons colored by concentration at a specified timestep.

docs.title: Signature
docs.text:
simulation.static_plot(
    plotting_timestep,
    constituent_name=None,
    clim=(None, None),
    cmap="RdYlBu_r",
    crs=None,
    save=False,
    output_path=None,
)

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type Description plotting_timestep integer Integer timestep index to plot. constituent_name string Name of the constituent to plot. Defaults to the first constituent. clim tuple Color bar limits as (min, max). Each entry may be None to use the constituent's auto-calculated min or max. cmap string Matplotlib colormap. Defaults to RdYlBu_r. crs string Coordinate reference system of the HEC-RAS project (for example, EPSG:26917). Required on the first plotting call to build the cell polygon geodataframe. save bool When True, save the figure to output_path. output_path string Filesystem path for the saved figure.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
simulation.static_plot(
    plotting_timestep=48,
    constituent_name="ecoli",
    clim=(0, 5000),
    cmap="viridis",
    crs="EPSG:26917",
    save=True,
    output_path="figures/ecoli_t48.png",
)

Empty cells (cells with volume equal to zero) are filtered from the plot. Axis ticks are removed and the background is set to light gray to emphasize the concentration field.

docs.title: Dynamic Polygon Plot
docs.text: The plot method produces a HoloViews DynamicMap in which each cell polygon is colored by concentration and the user drives a time slider to animate the simulation. The method overlays the concentration field on a CartoLight tile source.

docs.title: Signature
docs.text:
simulation.plot(
    constituent_name=None,
    crs=None,
    clim=(None, None),
    cmap="OrRd",
    time_index_range=(0, -1),
    filter_empty=True,
)

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type Description constituent_name string Name of the constituent to plot. crs string Coordinate reference system of the HEC-RAS project. Required on the first call to build the cell polygon geodataframe. Subsequent calls reuse the cached geodataframe. clim tuple Color bar limits as (min, max). cmap string Colormap name recognized by Bokeh or Matplotlib. Defaults to OrRd. time_index_range tuple Tuple of (start_index, end_index) bounding the time slider. filter_empty bool When True, cells with zero volume are hidden.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
dmap = simulation.plot(
    constituent_name="ecoli",
    crs="EPSG:26917",
    clim=(0, 5000),
    cmap="viridis",
    time_index_range=(0, 96),
)
dmap

The returned object is a HoloViews DynamicMap. In JupyterLab the display renders the slider and map automatically.

Note

The plot method builds a geopandas.GeoDataFrame of cell polygons and reprojects it to EPSG:4326 for compatibility with the tile source. This step can take several seconds for large meshes but is performed only once per simulation.

docs.title: Quick Plot
docs.text: The quick_plot method produces a HoloViews scatter plot of cell centroids colored by concentration. The method bypasses polygon generation and tile sources, so it renders far faster than plot on large meshes.

docs.title: Signature
docs.text:
simulation.quick_plot(
    constituent_name=None,
    clim=(None, None),
    cmap="OrRd",
)

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type Description constituent_name string Name of the constituent to plot. clim tuple Color bar limits as (min, max). cmap string Colormap name. Defaults to OrRd.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
dmap = simulation.quick_plot(
    constituent_name="ecoli",
    clim=(0, 5000),
    cmap="plasma",
)
dmap

Use quick_plot as a development-time diagnostic. For final figures and presentations, prefer plot or static_plot.

docs.title: Value Ranges and Color Limits
docs.text:
ClearWater-Riverine computes a minimum and maximum value for each constituent from the mesh when a plotting method needs a default color range. These values are cached on the Constituent object as min_value and max_value. Call simulation.set_value_range() to precompute ranges for all constituents, or simulation.set_value_range(constituent_name=...) to compute the range for a single constituent.

The finalize method calls set_value_range automatically, so value ranges are always populated on a simulation that has been finalized.

docs.title: Saving Animations
docs.text:
To export a dynamic map as a file, render the HoloViews object with an appropriate backend renderer.

import holoviews as hv

hv.extension("bokeh")

dmap = simulation.plot(
    constituent_name="ecoli",
    crs="EPSG:26917",
    clim=(0, 5000),
)
hv.save(dmap, "figures/ecoli_animation.html")

For GIF export, use matplotlib animations built from successive static_plot calls, or use an external screen-capture tool against the HTML output.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• First call requires crs. Both plot and static_plot need a CRS on the first invocation to build the cell polygon geodataframe. Supply the HEC-RAS project CRS (for example, EPSG:26917 for UTM Zone 17N) on the first call; subsequent calls reuse the cached geodataframe.
  • Plots do not render in Jupyter. Confirm that the Bokeh HoloViews extension is active by running import holoviews as hv; hv.extension("bokeh") in the notebook. ClearWater-Riverine loads the extension on import, but some notebook configurations require an explicit second call.
  • Color bar saturates. Pass an explicit clim tuple to override the auto-calculated min and max, which may be dominated by a small number of extreme cells near a boundary.

docs.title: Post-Processing
docs.text: ClearWater-Riverine provides post-processing utilities for mass balance accounting, edge-wise mass flux recovery, and derived geometric quantities. These utilities operate on the mesh produced by a completed simulation or on a mesh loaded from a saved Zarr dataset. The utilities are implemented in src/clearwater_riverine/postproc_util.py.

docs.title: Mass Flux Recovery
docs.text:
Every call to ClearwaterRiverine.update records advective, diffusive, and total mass flux across every edge in the mesh. The fluxes are stored in three arrays on each Constituent:

Array Shape Description advection_mass_flux (time, nedge) Mass crossing each edge over the timestep due to advection. Signed by the HEC-RAS face convention. diffusion_mass_flux (time, nedge) Mass crossing each edge over the timestep due to diffusion. total_mass_flux (time, nedge) Sum of advective and diffusive mass flux.

Each entry represents the cumulative mass transport over one timestep (concentration units multiplied by the timestep duration and the face flow or diffusive flow). The sign convention follows the HEC-RAS face flow convention: positive values indicate transport from edges_face1 to edges_face2.

docs.title: Loaded Meshes
docs.text: When a simulation is reconstructed from a saved mesh via the mesh_file_path argument, mass fluxes are not yet populated. The post-processing utilities detect this and call _calculate_mass_flux to recompute the fluxes using the stored concentrations and advection and diffusion coefficients. You do not need to invoke this function directly; the mass balance utilities handle it automatically.

docs.title: Global Mass Balance
docs.text: The _mass_bal_global function computes a global mass balance for a single constituent across the entire domain and the entire simulation horizon. The function returns a pandas.DataFrame with one row per simulation and columns that quantify starting mass, ending mass, per-boundary flows and fluxes, and closure error.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
from clearwater_riverine.postproc_util import _mass_bal_global

df = _mass_bal_global(
    simulation=simulation,
    constituent_name="ecoli",
    boundary_data_path=None,
)

Pass boundary_data_path when the simulation was reconstructed from a saved mesh and the boundary data CSV is stored alongside the mesh file.

docs.title: Output Columns
docs.text: Column Description Vol_start Total domain volume at the first timestep. Mass_start Total constituent mass at the first timestep. Vol_end Total domain volume at the last timestep. Mass_end Total constituent mass at the last timestep. <bc_name>_vol Net volume exchanged across boundary <bc_name> over the simulation horizon. <bc_name>_mass Net mass exchanged across boundary <bc_name> over the simulation horizon. <bc_name>_in_vol Volume entering the domain across boundary <bc_name>. <bc_name>_in_mass Mass entering the domain across boundary <bc_name>. <bc_name>_out_vol Volume leaving the domain across boundary <bc_name>. <bc_name>_out_mass Mass leaving the domain across boundary <bc_name>. bcTotalVolInOutAll Sum of net boundary volume exchanges across all boundaries. bcTotalMassInOutAll Sum of net boundary mass exchanges across all boundaries. vol_end_calc Ending volume predicted by adding net boundary exchanges to starting volume. mass_end_calc Ending mass predicted by adding net boundary exchanges to starting mass. error_vol Difference between predicted and observed ending volume. prct_error_vol Volume closure error expressed as a percentage of inflow volume. error_mass Difference between predicted and observed ending mass. prct_error_mass Mass closure error expressed as a percentage of inflow mass.

docs.title: Interpreting Closure Error
docs.text:
A well-posed simulation should produce prct_error_mass values that are small compared to the total inflow. Persistently large closure error often indicates:

  • A boundary line that is present in the HEC-RAS plan but missing from the boundary data lookup.
  • A saved mesh that was not paired with the correct boundary data CSV.
  • HEC-RAS output with volumes that do not match the time-integrated face flows at the reported precision.

docs.title: Reference Mass Balance at 100 mg L-1
docs.text: The _mass_bal_global_100_Ans function performs the same accounting as _mass_bal_global but forces all concentrations (initial, boundary, and ending) to 100 mg L-1. The result represents a pure volumetric accounting expressed in mass units and serves as a reference for isolating volume closure error from transport error. Use this utility when diagnosing discrepancies between the HEC-RAS volume field and the time-integrated face flow field.

docs.title: Edge Vertical Area and Volume
docs.text:
Several post-processing workflows require the vertical area of each edge (face depth times face width) at each timestep. ClearWater-Riverine stores this quantity on the mesh and uses it internally when building the diffusion term. The value is available through the mesh variables exposed in clearwater_riverine.variables.

Cell volumes at each timestep are stored in simulation.mesh.volume with dimensions (time, nface). The real-cell volume at the first timestep is accessed with:

nreal_index = simulation.mesh.attrs["nreal"] + 1
vol_start = simulation.mesh.volume[0][0:nreal_index]
total_vol_start = vol_start.sum().values

docs.title: Working with the Boundary Data Table
docs.text:
The simulation.boundary_data attribute is a pandas.DataFrame that maps HEC-RAS boundary line names to the edge (face) indices that compose each line. The post-processing utilities consume this table to split edge-wise mass flux into per-boundary totals. The relevant columns are:

Column Description Name Boundary line name as it appears in the HEC-RAS plan. BC Line ID Integer identifier assigned by HEC-RAS to the boundary line. Face Index Edge index (nedge) in the ClearWater-Riverine mesh for a single face of the boundary line.

If you save a simulation with ClearwaterRiverine.finalize(save=True, output_filepath=...), the boundary data table is written to <output_filepath_stem>_boundary_data.csv in the output directory.

docs.title: Typical Workflow
docs.text:
A representative post-processing workflow starts from either a live simulation or a saved mesh.

from clearwater_riverine import ClearwaterRiverine
from clearwater_riverine.postproc_util import _mass_bal_global

# Load a previously saved simulation
simulation = ClearwaterRiverine(
    mesh_file_path="results/ohio_river.zarr",
    verbose=True,
)

# Global mass balance for a single constituent
mass_balance_df = _mass_bal_global(
    simulation=simulation,
    constituent_name="ecoli",
    boundary_data_path="results/ohio_river_boundary_data.csv",
)

print(mass_balance_df[["Mass_start", "Mass_end", "prct_error_mass"]])

Note

Post-processing utilities whose names begin with an underscore are considered internal to the current release. The public post-processing API is expected to stabilize in a future release; the underlying behavior described on this page is the intended long-term design.

docs.title: Transport Solver
docs.text: ClearWater-Riverine solves the two-dimensional, depth-averaged advection-diffusion equation on the HEC-RAS 2D unstructured mesh using an implicit finite volume scheme. This page describes the governing equation, the spatial and temporal discretization, the sparse linear solve, and the per-timestep update procedure. The solver is implemented in src/clearwater_riverine/transport.py and src/clearwater_riverine/linalg.py.

docs.title: Governing Equation
docs.text:
For a scalar constituent with concentration C, cell volume V, face flow Q, and diffusion coefficient D, the depth-averaged transport equation integrated over one cell is:

\[ \frac{\partial (V C)}{\partial t} + \sum_{\text{faces}} (Q C)_{\text{upwind}} - \sum_{\text{faces}} D A_f \frac{C_{\text{nbr}} - C}{L_f} = 0 \]

where A_f is the vertical area of the face, L_f is the distance between the centers of the two cells sharing the face, and the subscript upwind indicates that the advected concentration is taken from the cell on the upwind side of the face.

docs.title: Finite Volume Discretization
docs.text: ClearWater-Riverine integrates the transport equation over each cell in the mesh. The spatial operator assembles contributions from every edge.

docs.title: Advection
docs.text:
The advection term uses a first-order upwind scheme. For each edge connecting cell i and cell j with face flow Q_ij:

  • If Q_ij > 0 (flow from i to j), the advected concentration is C_i.
  • If Q_ij < 0 (flow from j to i), the advected concentration is C_j.

The upwind choice is stored as the ADVECTION_COEFFICIENT variable on the mesh, with sign indicating the flow direction. Upwinding ensures monotonicity but introduces numerical diffusion proportional to the cell size and the flow speed.

docs.title: Diffusion
docs.text:
The diffusion term uses a standard two-point flux approximation. For each edge between cells i and j:

\[ F_{\text{diff}} = D A_f \frac{C_j - C_i}{L_f} \]

ClearWater-Riverine computes D A_f / L_f once during mesh preparation and stores the result as COEFFICIENT_TO_DIFFUSION_TERM on the mesh. The diffusion coefficient D is the scalar diffusion_coefficient from the configuration.

docs.title: Volume Change
docs.text: The time derivative partial (V C) / partial t is expanded to account for the time-varying cell volume supplied by HEC-RAS. The framework stores VOLUME at every timestep and CHANGE_IN_TIME as the timestep duration. Volume changes enter the discretization as contributions to both the diagonal of the left-hand side matrix and the right-hand side vector.

docs.title: Implicit Time Stepping
docs.text:
ClearWater-Riverine uses a fully implicit (backward Euler) time discretization. At each timestep n, the framework assembles and solves:

\[ A\, C^{n+1} = b^n \]

where A is a sparse matrix of size (nreal + 1, nreal + 1) built from the advection and diffusion coefficients and the current cell volumes, and b^n is a vector built from the concentrations at timestep n, boundary inflows at timestep n+1, and the previous cell volumes.

The implicit scheme is unconditionally stable with respect to advection and diffusion. The timestep is inherited from the HEC-RAS output, so the modeler controls stability and accuracy by choosing the HEC-RAS output interval rather than a separate transport timestep.

docs.title: Sparse Linear Solve
docs.text:
ClearWater-Riverine builds A as a compressed sparse row (CSR) matrix using scipy.sparse.csr_matrix and solves the system with scipy.sparse.linalg.spsolve. The framework constructs the matrix from three parallel arrays.

Array Contents lhs.coef Matrix coefficients (advection, diffusion, and volume terms). lhs.rows Row indices for each coefficient. lhs.cols Column indices for each coefficient.

The LHS class in src/clearwater_riverine/linalg.py exposes an update_values(mesh, t) method that refreshes the three arrays using the flow field at timestep t. Because the matrix depends only on flow and geometry, ClearWater-Riverine assembles A once per timestep and reuses it across all constituents.

Each constituent owns its own right-hand side vector through the RHS class. The right-hand side is updated per constituent per timestep via b.update_values(solution, mesh, t, name).

docs.title: Ghost Cells
docs.text: HEC-RAS boundary faces connect real cells to ghost cells that live outside the domain. ClearWater-Riverine indexes ghost cells after the real cells, so the total cell count is nreal + nghost. The matrix A has dimension (nreal + 1, nreal + 1) and represents the real cells plus one slot used to apply boundary concentrations. The additional slot receives concentration values taken directly from the aligned boundary condition time series, so boundary inflows appear in A x = b as known forcing rather than as unknowns.

docs.title: Per-Timestep Update Procedure
docs.text:
The update method on the ClearwaterRiverine class advances the solution one timestep. The procedure is:

  1. Refresh the left-hand side arrays for the current timestep with self.lhs.update_values(mesh, time_step).
  2. Build A = csr_matrix(...) with shape (nreal + 1, nreal + 1).
  3. For each constituent: a. Optionally override the current concentration with a user-supplied value passed via the update_concentration dictionary. This is the hook used by the ClearWater Modules coupling pattern to inject updated state between transport steps. b. Refresh the right-hand side vector using constituent.b.update_values(...). c. Solve x = spsolve(A, constituent.b.vals). d. Write x into the mesh at time_step + 1. e. Overwrite cells that carry nonzero boundary condition inputs with the boundary concentration. f. Compute advective, diffusive, and total mass flux across every edge and store the values on the mesh.
  4. Increment self.time_step by one.

The mass flux recovery in step 3f reconstructs edge-wise fluxes using the newly solved concentrations, the ADVECTION_COEFFICIENT field, and the COEFFICIENT_TO_DIFFUSION_TERM field. These fluxes are used by the post-processing utilities; see Post-Processing.

docs.title: Running to Completion
docs.text:
A typical simulation loops update across the HEC-RAS time axis and then calls finalize to set plot value ranges and optionally save the mesh.

from clearwater_riverine import ClearwaterRiverine

simulation = ClearwaterRiverine(
    config_filepath="configs/ohio_river.yml",
    verbose=True,
)

for _ in range(len(simulation.mesh.time) - 1):
    simulation.update()

simulation.finalize(
    save=True,
    output_filepath="results/ohio_river.zarr",
)

The finalize call writes the ClearWater-Riverine mesh to Zarr and the boundary data to a companion CSV. The saved mesh can be reloaded later for post-processing and plotting by passing mesh_file_path to the ClearwaterRiverine constructor.

docs.title: Numerical Considerations
docs.text:
• Mass conservation. The implicit finite volume scheme is mass-conservative to the accuracy of the linear solve. Residual mass balance error reported by the post-processing utilities typically reflects accumulated floating point error and any mismatch between HEC-RAS face flows and volume changes.
  • Numerical diffusion. First-order upwinding introduces artificial diffusion. If the physical diffusion coefficient is small relative to numerical diffusion, the transport solution will appear more diffuse than the underlying problem warrants. Refining the mesh reduces numerical diffusion.
  • Negative concentrations. The implicit upwind scheme is monotone in the absence of steep boundary transients. If negative concentrations appear, check for sharp boundary condition discontinuities and for HEC-RAS cells with very small or zero volume.

docs.title: Temperature Simulation Module (TSM)
docs.text: The Temperature Simulation Module (TSM) computes water temperature in rivers, reservoirs, and other surface waters by solving a surface energy balance at each computational cell. TSM couples to external transport models (for example, HEC-RAS 2D) that supply hydrodynamics; TSM itself computes only the thermodynamic source and sink terms and advances water temperature in time.

docs.title: In This Section
docs.text:
• Overview describes what TSM simulates, which heat exchange processes it represents, and how it is coupled to a transport model.
  • Energy Balance documents each heat flux term and the governing equations TSM uses to update water temperature.
  • Configuration lists the static parameters (wind function coefficients, sediment properties, time step) and meteorological inputs required to run TSM.

docs.title: Related Theory
docs.text: See the Temperature page in the Theory section for the underlying derivation of the surface energy balance and the physical assumptions built into TSM.

docs.title: TSM Configuration
docs.text: This page describes the parameters required to configure TSM for a simulation. The parameters fall into four groups: wind function coefficients, sediment thermal properties, numerical controls, and meteorological forcing.

docs.title: Wind Function Coefficients
docs.text:
The latent and sensible heat fluxes share a common wind function:

\[ f(U_w) = a + b \, U_w^c \]

The user supplies the three coefficients. Typical values come from the QUAL2K, CE-QUAL-W2, and EPA stream temperature literature.

Parameter Units Description Typical Value a_wind W m\(^{-2}\) mbar\(^{-1}\) Linear wind function constant 6.9 b_wind W m\(^{-2}\) mbar\(^{-1}\) (m s\(^{-1}\))\(^{-c}\) Wind speed multiplier 0.345 c_wind dimensionless Wind speed exponent 1.0

Note
